cards.x: Install the add-on first, then the content pack, then the biomes. Everything is set up in Blender's Preferences.

In Preferences, open the Get Extensions page and choose Install from Disk from the arrow menu in its top-right corner. Pick the .zip file you downloaded. Once it is installed, ScatterFlow is in the 3D viewport's sidebar. Press N to open it. Requires Blender 5.2 or newer. ScatterFlow Nano needs the ScatterFlow build of Blender. It is in beta, so keep backups of your files. If Windows blocks it the first time, choose More info, then Run anyway.
The content pack contains the models and textures that ScatterFlow uses.

Asset libraries are the folders ScatterFlow loads its models from. Click the Add asset library button and pick a folder for the content pack. Then click the Install asset libraries button and choose the content pack. Needs 7-Zip or WinRAR. The content pack is a .rar archive, which Blender cannot open on its own. If you have neither program, install 7-Zip (free) first.

Other asset libraries are added the same way. If a library is already installed on your computer, just add its folder. Removing a library from the list does not delete its files. To browse these models in Blender's Asset Browser as well, see Adding the library.

cards.t: When the content does not install
cards.x: A part of the archive is missing. Keep both parts of the content pack in the same folder. The archive could not be extracted. A download is probably incomplete. Download it again. Not enough disk space. The installed content pack needs about 6 GB. “This is a biome pack.” Install it from the Biomes section instead. Running the install again repairs an incomplete install.
Biomes are ready-made scatter setups. They use the models from the content pack, so install that first.

Choose a folder for your biomes with the folder button in the Biomes section. Then click the Install biome packs button and choose the biome pack. The biomes then appear in the Biome Browser. The icon next to the folder shows whether your biomes have everything they need. If it shows a warning, hover over it to see what is missing. Updating a biome pack. The installer does not overwrite existing files. To update a pack, delete its folder first, then install the new version.

cards.t: When the biomes do not appear
cards.x: The icon shows a warning. Hover over it to see which asset library is missing, then add it under Asset Libraries. “This is an asset library.” Install it from the Asset Libraries section instead. The Biome Browser is empty. Make sure the biome folder is the one you installed into, then refresh the browser. For GScatter environments and your own biomes, see Installing biome packs.
The rest of the preferences are in the Settings panel. Click its header to expand it.

Density 1Scale 1Random Scale onRandom Rotation onAlign to Surface offBounding Box off These set how new scatter layers start: their Density and Scale, and which features are turned on. Existing layers are not affected. Turn on Bounding Box to show new layers as boxes in the viewport, which keeps heavy scenes fast. See Optimized Mesh. If Blender does not save preferences automatically, click the Save Preferences button in the lower-left corner.
Refreshes the layer list when you switch scenes. It is experimental, so only turn it on if you work across several scenes.
The Export and Megascans panels hold the settings for game engine export and Megascans. Leave the Debug Logging checkbox off unless support asks you to turn it on.

cards.t: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.s: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: The content pack has plants, rocks, props, and effects. The biomes use them, but you can also add them one at a time from Blender's Asset Browser.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: To see the content pack in the Asset Browser, add its folder to Blender's own asset libraries once. This is separate from ScatterFlow's Asset Libraries, which tell biomes where to find their models.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: In Edit > Preferences, open Asset Libraries, click the + button, and choose the ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack folder. Pick the folder itself, not a file inside it. Set the Import Method menu to Append, so assets you add become editable copies in your file. The library then appears in the library menu of every Asset Browser. Update the path after moving the library. If the assets disappear after you move the folder, set the Path field here to its new location.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: Open an Asset Browser, for example by switching the Timeline to one, and choose ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack from the library menu. The catalogs sort the assets into Foliage, Ivy, Trash & Debris, Water, Weather, and Atmosphere. Ivy holds the leaves, flowers, and presets for the Ivy tools. Click a catalog to filter the assets, or expand it to browse its subcategories. The Search field finds assets by name. Initial loading may take longer. The library is large, so previews can take a moment to appear the first time.

cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: Drag an asset into the 3D viewport. It lands on the surface under your cursor. Most assets hold several variations, which arrive in a row inside a collection named after the asset. Move them around or delete the ones you do not need. Materials are included. Use Material Preview or Rendered shading to see the textures. For props you place by hand, Randomize Transform adds variety and Snap to Ground places them on the terrain.

cards.t: From an asset to a scatter layer
cards.pt: Content pack and the Asset Browser
cards.x: An asset's collection of variations can be scattered directly. Drag the asset into the scene, choose an Emitter in the ScatterFlow panel, and click the + button to add a layer. In the Instances section, set the Type menu to Multiple Instances and pick the asset's collection. Then raise Density / m² to fill the surface with its variations. From there, adjust the layer like any other, with Scale, Rotation, masks, and Wind. Supported content pack materials also respond to the season, snow, and dryness settings. You can hide the original objects or move them out of view, but keep them in the file. The layer uses them as its source.

ScatterFlow turns your Megascans downloads into ready-to-use Blender assets, with their materials already set up. They are saved in the Megascans_SF asset library, so you can use them from the Asset Browser in any Blender file.
Choose a library location before installing your first asset.

The Megascans settings are in ScatterFlow's add-on preferences, in the Megascans section of the Settings panel. Set the Folder field to where you want to keep your Megascans assets, then click the Register / Refresh Asset Library button. Pick a location with room for both the extracted downloads and the finished Blender assets. See The settings, one by one for details on each option.
The Megascans panel has two settings and a button that registers the library.

Where all your installed Megascans content is kept. You need to choose a folder before you can install anything. Inside it, the Assets folder holds one .blend file per asset, sorted by type. These are what the Asset Browser shows. SourceFiles holds the extracted downloads with their full-resolution textures. The materials use these textures, so do not delete this folder. blender_assets.cats.txt stores the Asset Browser catalogs. One extracted download can take several hundred megabytes. To move the library, move the whole folder, update the Folder field, and click the Register / Refresh Asset Library button.

Default Off Some Megascans downloads include several levels of detail (LODs). LOD0 is the most detailed model, and each higher number has fewer polygons. Off: installs only the most detailed model, which keeps the files smaller. Use it when you render in Blender. On: installs every LOD into the same asset, and the asset's description lists which ones it has. Use it when you also need lighter models for distant scattering or game engines. The setting only applies when you install. It does not change existing assets, so install a download again to change its LODs.

Registers your folder in Blender as the Megascans_SF asset library. It creates the folder and the Megascans catalogs if they are missing, and saves your preferences so the library is still there after you restart Blender. The library uses the Append import method, so assets you add to a scene are editable copies. Installing an asset does all of this too. Use the button when you first set up, after changing the Folder field, or if the library is missing from the Asset Browser.

Click the Install Megascans button in the header of an Asset Browser and choose one or more downloaded Megascans .zip files. You can also browse into a Megascans folder you have already extracted. Any editor, such as the Timeline, can be switched to an Asset Browser. Installed assets are in the Megascans_SF library, sorted into its Megascans catalogs. Asset not visible? Click the refresh arrows beside the library menu.

Drag an asset from the Asset Browser into the viewport. It becomes an ordinary object that you can move, edit, or scatter. Its material is already set up with the textures that came with it, such as colour, roughness, normal, and displacement. Assets are appended, not linked, so editing one in your scene does not change the library copy. To scatter it, choose it in a layer's Instances section.

The installer detects each download's type and puts it in the matching catalog. 3D assets and 3D plants become model assets. A download with several variations becomes one asset that holds them all. Dragging it into a scene brings in every variation, ready to use together in a scatter layer. Surfaces, decals, imperfections, atlases, and brushes have only textures, so they become material assets. Drag one onto an object to apply it. Supported model formats are FBX, OBJ, glTF, USD, Alembic, PLY, and STL. Supported texture formats are JPG, PNG, TIFF, EXR, TGA, BMP, WebP, and HDR.

The material is built from the download's textures, recognised by filename. All the common maps are supported, including colour, roughness or gloss, normal, displacement, opacity, and translucency. The highest-resolution version of each texture is used. Opacity maps give cutout materials for leaves and grass. With a displacement map, the material uses Displacement and Bump. In Cycles, the surface is displaced when the mesh has enough geometry; otherwise it adds bump detail.

Installing an asset again replaces its .blend file and its files in SourceFiles. Use this to change its LODs or to repair it. Objects already in your scenes are separate copies, so they are not updated.

“Choose an Asset Library folder first.” Set the Folder field in the Megascans preferences. See Install location. “Select a Megascans ZIP, or browse into a Megascans folder.” Select the .zip files themselves, or open an extracted Megascans folder and click the Install Megascans button without selecting a file. “No supported mesh or Megascans texture maps were found in that source.” No model or texture files were recognised. Check that it is a supported Megascans download. “Installed 2 of 3 source(s). 1 failed; see System Console.” Some downloads in a batch failed. Choose Window > Toggle System Console from Blender's top menu to see why.

An emitter is the object a scatter setup belongs to, usually a terrain. Choose one to see its layers and the rest of the Scatter tab.

Choose an object in the Emitter field, or pick one in the viewport with the eyedropper. Each emitter has its own layer list. Use separate emitters to organize scattering across several terrains, such as a meadow and a hill. Switching emitters only changes which list you are editing. Layers on other emitters stay active in the scene.

A layer is one scatter setup: the objects it places, their density, and the masks and settings that control them. The System List shows the current emitter's layers, and the settings below it apply to the selected layer.

Click + beside the System List to add a layer, then choose its objects in the Instances section. Double-click a layer's name to rename it. Clear names, such as Rocks, make the list easier to read. New layers start with the density, scale, and rotation defaults from the add-on preferences. Object Mode required. Switch Blender to Object Mode before adding a layer.

The monitor icon shows or hides a layer in the viewport, and the camera icon does the same for renders. Hide heavy layers in the viewport but keep them on for rendering, so the scene stays easy to work with. The colour swatch is only a label to help you tell layers apart. It does not change how they look in the scene.

Choose Duplicate Layer from the arrow menu below the list buttons to copy the selected layer with all its settings. The copy places instances in the same spots as the original. Change its Seed for a new arrangement, or choose different objects to reuse the layout with another asset.
Select a layer, click −, and confirm. This removes the layer and its instances, but not the original objects.
Click a row to edit that layer. Use the up and down arrows to reorder layers and keep related ones together.

Both are in the same arrow menu as Duplicate Layer. Choose Refresh List from that menu to bring the System List up to date with the current scene. Use it if the list still shows layers from another scene after you switch. Turn on Auto Refresh to do this automatically when the scene changes.
A group is a folder for several layers. It lets you hide, duplicate, or adjust them together.

cards.t: Create a group and fill it
cards.x: Click the folder button beside the System List to create an empty group, and double-click its name to rename it. To add a layer, select it and click + on the group's row. Adding a layer to a group does not change its own settings.

cards.t: The buttons on a group row
cards.x: The triangle opens or closes the group. The eye shows or hides every layer in the group, in both the viewport and renders. The − button on a grouped layer's row takes that layer out of the group. The group stays, even when it is empty. The duplicate icon copies the group with all its layers. Deleting a group preserves its layers. Select the group and click the System List's − button. Only the folder is removed, and its layers move back to the top level of the list.
Select a group to see the Group Scattering section instead of the layer's Scattering section. Its controls affect every layer in the group, while each layer keeps its own Density and Seed.

Default 100% Multiplies every layer's density by the same percentage. 100% leaves them unchanged, 50% halves them, and 200% doubles them. Use it to thin out or fill in a whole biome while keeping the balance between trees, bushes, rocks, and other layers.

Default 0 Shifts every layer's seed by the same amount. This gives the group a new arrangement, while each layer keeps its own seed and its own pattern. Set it back to 0 to return to the original arrangement.

Default ProceduralGroup Spread 5.00 Switches every layer in the group between Procedural and Manual. In Manual, the Start Placing button paints all the group's layers at once, so you can place a mix of trees, bushes, and rocks in one stroke. Group Spread sets how far apart the layers place their instances around the brush. Lower values keep them close together; higher values spread them out. See Manual Mode for the brush controls.
Selecting a group also shows group versions of other sections, such as Group Surface and Group Scale. These are covered on their own feature pages.
Surface, Instances, and Scattering are the first three sections below the System List. They all apply to the selected layer.
Choose what the layer scatters on: the emitter itself, another object, or a collection of objects.

Default Emitter Object In the Type menu, Emitter Object scatters on the current emitter. Single Surface scatters on another object you choose. Use it to put a layer on one surface, such as a boulder, without changing its emitter. Multiple Surfaces scatters on every object in a collection. For example, choose a collection of boulders to cover the rocks and leave the terrain around them clear. Whatever surface it uses, the layer stays in its emitter's System List. Collection missing from the picker? Multiple Surfaces only lists collections directly under the Scene Collection. Move a nested collection up to that level to use it.
Choose the objects the layer places on its surface.
Scatters one object. Choose it in the field below Type, or pick it with the eyedropper. Swapping the object keeps the same positions, so you can compare a tree, rock, or bush in the same layout.

Set Type to Multiple Instances to scatter a mix of objects from a collection. Each point uses one of the collection's objects. Add or remove objects in the collection to change the mix. The layer updates automatically.
Choose how instances are placed, how many there are, and how far apart they sit.

Default Procedural Procedural spreads instances across the surface based on settings such as Density and masks. It updates whenever you change a setting. Manual starts empty and lets you place instances with brushes. Click the Start Placing button in the Manual Mode section, which takes the place of Density and the Factor buttons. See Manual Mode for the brushes. Use Procedural for coverage that follows changes to your setup, and Manual for deliberate placement, such as a hero tree or a path edge. To combine both, make one layer of each with the same objects. Switching modes preserves manual placements. Going back to Procedural restores the automatic scatter, and switching to Manual again brings back your hand-placed instances.
Sets how many instances are placed per square metre of surface, before any masks remove some. Use higher values for small plants and lower values for trees.

Default 0 Changes the random arrangement without changing how many instances there are. Type a value, or click the dice for a random one. Give separate layers different seeds so they do not place instances in the same spots.

Default 2.00 Sets the step used by the four Density buttons: multiply, divide, add, and subtract. With Factor at 2, * doubles Density and / halves it. + and − add or subtract the Factor itself, so use a small Factor, such as 0.1, on sparse layers.

Default offMinimum Distance 0 m Keeps instances in the same layer a minimum distance apart. Set Minimum Distance to the closest they may be. Instances that are too close are removed, so a larger Minimum Distance means fewer instances. At large values, spacing rather than Density decides how many you get. It only checks the current layer. To space out different layers, use Ecosystem.

Manual Mode lets you place instances by hand, such as a hero tree, plants along a path, or the edge of a clearing. Set the layer's Scattering Type to Manual to open the Manual Mode section. See Scattering Type for how it compares with Procedural mode.

cards.t: Start Placing and the mode dials
cards.x: Click Start Placing to show the brush dials in the viewport. Pick a brush by clicking its dial or pressing its number, 1–9. Nothing is placed until you pick one. Click the active dial again to get back to the full brush list. Press Esc, Enter, or right-click to leave Manual Mode. Your placements stay on the layer.
Choose which objects the placement brushes can use.

The list shows the objects from the layer's Instances section. Untick an object to leave it out of new placements, for example to paint only the trees from a mixed collection. The All button ticks every object; the None button unticks them all. Enable at least one object. Start Placing cannot begin when every object is disabled.

Hold Ctrl and drag to erase instances. The exceptions are Scale, where Ctrl shrinks instances, and Attract, where it pushes them away. Hold F and move the mouse sideways to change the brush size. This is the same as the Radius dial. You can still move around the viewport while painting.

Drag a dial sideways to change its value. Hold Shift for finer control, or scroll the mouse wheel over the dial. Ctrl+click or double-click resets a dial. Click an on/off dial to toggle it. Every brush has a Radius dial. It starts at 2.0, or 0.7 for Precision.

Density 1Delay 1.00Surface Rotation on Places random instances inside the brush as you drag. Density is how many instances each step of the stroke adds. Delay is the distance between steps, not a time. Low values give a continuous band; high values give separate clusters. Surface Rotation tilts new instances to match the slope. Turn it off to keep them upright.

Scale 1.00Mesh Preview on Places one instance at a time. Press and drag to position it, then release to place it. Scale sets the size of the next instance. Click the Swap Preview dial, or press F8, to switch to another object. It works when the layer uses a collection with more than one object ticked in Scatter Manager. Mesh Preview shows a see-through preview of the object at the cursor. Turn it off to show a simple ring instead.

Density 1Delay 1.00Surface Rotation on Works like Area, but turns each instance to face along the stroke. Use it for fences, logs, hedges, or crop rows. Density, Delay, and Surface Rotation work as in Area, but Align keeps its own values.
These brushes change the instances you have placed by hand on the active layer. Other layers are not affected.

Adjust Normals off Drag to move instances across the surface. The brush picks up whatever is inside it when you start dragging, so make Radius big enough to cover the whole group. Turn on Adjust Normals to tilt moved instances to match the slope at their new spot.

Scale Speed 0.05 Hold the mouse button over instances to grow them, or hold Ctrl to shrink them. Scaling keeps going while you hold the button, so use short presses for small changes. Scale Speed sets how fast they grow or shrink.
Jitter 0.10 Adds random tilt to instances under the brush, building up the longer you stay over them. Use it to break up an arrangement that looks too even. Jitter sets how much tilt each step adds.

Probability 0.10Min Distance 0.70 Thins out crowded areas by removing instances that are too close together. Min Distance is the spacing you want. Instances closer than this may be removed. Probability is the chance that each of those instances is removed on a pass. Low values thin gradually over several strokes; high values remove more at once.

Pull Speed 0.03Adjust Normals off Hold the mouse button to pull instances toward the cursor. The longer you hold, the tighter the cluster, until they can all end up on the same spot. Hold Ctrl to push them out to the edge of the brush instead, which is handy for opening a clearing. Increase Radius to affect a larger area. Pull Speed sets how fast they move. Turn on Adjust Normals to keep them aligned to the surface as they move.
Rotate Speed 0.015 Leans instances in the direction you stroke. Use it to flatten grass or give trees a wind-blown look. Rotate Speed sets how strongly each stroke changes the lean.
Set a group's Type to Manual to paint all its layers together. Group Spread sets how far apart the layers are placed around the brush. See Group Scattering.
Scale has three controls that you turn on separately: overall size, size per axis, and random variation. Their values multiply, so you can use them together.

Default on, 1.0 Scales every instance by the same amount. 1 keeps the object's original size, 2 doubles it, and 0.5 halves it. Turn it off to remove its effect without losing the value. The starting value for new layers is set in the add-on preferences.

Default off, 1 / 1 / 1 Scales instances separately along X, Y, and Z. Raise Z to make objects taller, or change X and Y to change their width. Use it for taller grass or flatter rocks without editing the original mesh.

New layers onMin 0.6Max 1Seed 0 Gives each instance a random size between Min and Max, as a multiple of the original size. Lower Min for more variation; values near 0 give many very small instances. Set Max above 1 to allow instances larger than the original. The Random Scale checkbox in the preferences sets whether new layers start with it on; see Defaults. Seed changes which instances get which size, without changing the range.
When you select a group, Group Scale takes the place of the Scale section. Its Uniform Scale applies to every layer in the group.
Rotation combines a fixed rotation, alignment to the surface, and random variation. These controls work on single layers, not groups.

Default off, 0° / 0° / 0° Rotates every instance by the same amount around X, Y, and Z. Z turns its heading; X and Y tilt it. Use it to fix an object that faces the wrong way, or to lean a whole layer in one direction.

Default Amount 0 / 0 / 1Seed 0 Gives each instance a different random rotation. The three Amount values set how much it varies around X, Y, and Z. The default spins instances freely around Z and keeps them upright, which suits most plants. Add X and Y for rocks or debris that should tilt in any direction. Seed gives a different set of rotations. The add-on preferences set whether new layers start with Random Rotation on.

Default offMax Angle 90° Limits Random Rotation to steps of Max Angle. Which step each instance gets is still random. At 90° instances face one of four directions, at 45° one of eight, and at 180° one of two. Use it for objects that should stay neatly lined up, such as crates, paving, or planks.

Default set in preferencesAlignment Strength 1.0 Tilts each instance to match the surface under it, so on a slope it leans with the ground. Alignment Strength blends from upright at 0 to fully aligned at 1. Around 0–0.3 suits trees that should stay mostly upright. 1 suits grass, rocks, and anything that should follow the ground closely.
Paint a vertex group on the scatter surface to choose where a layer appears. Instances stay in painted areas and are removed everywhere else.

Default off Turn on Vertex Group and pick a group. You can keep several groups and switch between them to try different layouts. The list shows the vertex groups on the layer's surface: its emitter, or its Single Surface object. Mask detail depends on the surface mesh. Weights are stored per vertex, so a coarse mesh gives a rough edge. Subdivide the area when you need finer control.
Select the surface object and click the brush button at the end of the row to start weight painting. Paint where the layer should appear. Click the button again to go back to Object Mode.

Default offTransition 1.0 Without Smooth Transition, instances are either kept or removed. With it on, instances get smaller where the paint is lighter, so the edge of the mask fades out. Transition sets how much paint an instance needs to reach full size. Lower values reach full size in lightly painted areas. Higher values need heavier paint.

Default off Reverses the mask, so the layer appears outside the painted area. The arrow button next to the vertex group field does the same. This lets one mask serve several layers. For example, paint a path, use it as it is for gravel or flowers, and invert it on a tree layer to keep trees off the path.
Use nearby objects to keep a layer away from them, or only close to them. For example, clear space around boulders, or grow plants along walls and around tree stumps.

Default offDistance 0 m Turn on Geometry Proximity, pick an object in the Object field, and set a Distance. By default, instances within that distance are removed. Distance is measured from the object's surface, not its centre, so the cleared area follows its shape.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the edge of the cleared area. Instances grow from nothing at the Distance edge to full size Transition metres further out.

Default Avoid Set Behaviour to Avoid to remove instances within the Distance of the object. Set it to Seek to keep instances only within that Distance. Use it to gather plants around something, such as weeds at the foot of a wall or ferns around a stump.

cards.t: Type: Single Object or Multiple Objects
cards.x: Default Single Object Set Type to Single Object to use one object. Set it to Multiple Objects to use a collection instead, which applies the same settings to every object in it.
Use a curve to shape a path, road, stream, fence line, or any other long boundary. The scatter updates as you edit the curve.
Default offDistance 1 m Turn on Curve Proximity and pick a curve in the Curve field. With Avoid, Distance is the clearance on each side of the curve, so set it to half the width of your path.
Default offTransition 2 Fades the edge of the path. Instances grow to full size over the Transition distance instead of stopping abruptly.

Default off Distance is normally measured in 3D. If the curve sits too far above the terrain, its effect weakens or disappears, and the path can close up. Turn on Infinite Z to ignore height, so the curve affects the ground directly below it. This lets you shape a path on uneven terrain with a flat curve above the ground.
Default Avoid Set Behaviour to Avoid to clear instances along the curve. Set it to Seek to keep them only near the curve, which suits hedges, tree-lined avenues, or reeds along a stream.

cards.t: Type: Single Curve or Multiple Curves
cards.x: Default Single Curve Set Type to Single Curve to use one curve. Set it to Multiple Curves to use a collection, so one set of settings can control a whole network of paths.

Ecosystem lets one layer react to another layer's instances, such as bushes growing around the boulders of a rock layer. Set it up on the layer you want to control, and choose the layer it should follow or avoid. The other layer is not changed. When its arrangement changes, for example after a new seed, the reacting layer follows.

Default offDistance 0 m Turn on Attraction and choose the layer to follow in the Scatter System field. Instances are kept only within Distance of that layer's instances. A lower Distance gives smaller, tighter patches, such as bushes close to each boulder. A Distance of 0 leaves the layer empty. Distance starts at 0, so raise it after turning Attraction on.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the outer edge of each patch. Instances stay full size up to Distance, then shrink to zero over the next Transition metres.
Default offDistance 0 m Removes instances within Distance of the other layer and keeps them everywhere else. Use it to keep grass out of rocks, or to clear small plants from around large trees.
Default offTransition 1 m Softens the edge of the cleared area. Instances grow from zero size at Distance to full size Transition metres further out.

You can turn on Attraction and Repulsion together, pointing at the same layer or at two different ones. On the same layer, set Repulsion's Distance smaller than Attraction's to get a ring around each instance. Bushes then stay near the boulders without sitting right beside them. On different layers, one pulls the layer in and the other keeps it away. Use this for moss that grows near rocks but stays away from trees.
Select a group to see Group Ecosystem. Its settings apply to every layer in the group, so a whole planting can follow or avoid another layer together.

The Abiotic section of the Scatter tab has three masks that place a layer by the shape of the terrain: its slope, its height, and the direction it faces. Each layer has its own masks, and you can combine all three. These masks hide instances by shrinking them to zero. A smooth transition therefore makes instances smaller near the edge, rather than fewer.
Keeps a layer on flatter ground, or on steeper ground when inverted. Use it to keep trees on terraces and off cliff faces.

Default 0.85Range 0 to 1 Sets how flat the ground must be for the layer to appear. 1 is level ground and 0 is a vertical wall. Raise Slope to keep the layer on flatter ground. Lower it to allow steeper slopes. As a guide, 0.85 allows slopes up to about 32°, 0.7 about 45°, and 0.5 about 60°.

Default offTransition 0.5 Fades instance size across the slope edge. Instances are zero size at the cutoff and reach full size on ground that is flatter by the Transition amount. A small Transition gives a narrow band of smaller instances. A larger one spreads the band further onto flat ground. Keep Slope + Transition at or below 1. Ground cannot be flatter than 1, so with a higher total, instances never reach full size. At the defaults of 0.85 and 0.5, even level ground only reaches 30% scale. A Transition of 0.05–0.15 is a good place to start.

Default off Reverses the mask, so the layer stays on steep ground and off flat ground. With Invert on, lowering Slope keeps the layer on steeper and steeper surfaces. For example, use an inverted mask for rocks or scree on a cliff, next to a plant layer with the same Slope that is not inverted.
Limits a layer by height. Use it for boundaries such as a mountain tree line.

Default 5 m Sets the highest point the layer reaches. Without Smooth Transition, instances above it are removed. Height is measured along the scene's Z axis, so check where your terrain sits, especially if it is far above or below zero. Layer disappears after enabling the mask? The default cutoff is 5 m. If your whole emitter is higher than that, raise Height until the layer shows.

Default offTransition 5 Fades instances out above the cutoff. They stay full size up to Height, then shrink to zero over the next Transition metres. Use a short transition for a sharp tree line, or a long one for a gradual edge.

Default off Keeps instances above the cutoff instead of below it, so Height becomes the layer's lower limit. Use it for high-altitude plants or rocks near a snow line. Two layers with the same Height, one inverted and one not, split a terrain into upper and lower areas.

Default offAmount 55Scale 0.2 Adds noise to the height cutoff, so the edge does not follow a flat line. Amount sets how far the cutoff can move. At 0 it does not move. The default of 55 suits large terrains; lower it on smaller terrain, where the effect can be too strong. Scale sets the size of the pattern. Lower values give broad changes along the edge; higher values give smaller, more frequent ones.
Limits a layer by the direction a slope faces. Use it for moss on shaded hillsides, or plants on slopes that face the sun.

Default 0° Sets the compass direction the slope must face, which decides the side of each hill the layer covers. Without Smooth Transition, instances are largest on steep slopes that face that direction, and get smaller toward the sides. Level ground faces no direction, so it stays empty at the default Offset.

Default 0 Widens or narrows the area the mask covers. Positive values keep the layer on steeper slopes facing the chosen angle. Negative values spread it further around the hill and onto level ground.

Default offTransition 0.5 Sets how gradually instances grow from zero to full size across the mask edge. Use a small Transition for full-size instances with a clear edge. Larger values give a wider, softer band of smaller instances. Enabling Smooth Transition slightly narrows the mask. Lower Offset to get the previous coverage back.
Texture masks use a pattern to control where instances appear and how they shrink near its edges. Each mask has its own checkbox, and you can combine several.
Creates irregular patches with gaps between them. Use it for plants that should grow in natural clumps instead of an even carpet.

Min 0.4Max 0.6 The noise has a value from 0 to 1 at each point. Instances are removed below Min, are full size above Max, and scale up gradually in between. Raise both values for less coverage, or lower them to fill more of the surface. Move them closer together for sharp edges, or further apart for a softer fade.

Seed 0Scale 1.0 Seed rearranges the patches without changing the other settings. Scale sets the size of the pattern. Lower values make fewer, larger patches. Higher values make more, smaller ones. On a large terrain, start with values around 0.1–0.3.

Detail 2Roughness 0.5Lacunarity 2Distortion 0 Detail adds smaller patterns on top of the main noise. At 0, the patch edges are smooth and rounded. Higher values make them more ragged. Roughness sets how strong the finer patterns are, and Lacunarity how much smaller each one gets. Both only work when Detail is above 0. Distortion warps the noise into swirls and stretched shapes.
Creates parallel rows. Use it for crops, vineyards, ploughed fields, or planted borders.
Min 0.3Max 0.6 These work as they do for Noise. Raising Min makes the planted rows narrower and the gaps wider. Max sets how instances fade to full size along the row edges.

Scale 0.6Phase Offset 0 Scale sets the number of rows. Lower values give fewer, wider rows. Higher values give more, narrower rows. Phase Offset slides the rows sideways without changing their spacing. Use it to line them up with a fence, path, or another layer.

Distortion 0Detail 2Detail Scale 1Detail Roughness 0.5 Distortion bends the rows, so the planting looks less straight and regular. The other settings shape that bending, and do nothing while Distortion is 0. Detail adds finer variation, Detail Scale sets its size, and Detail Roughness sets the strength of the finest changes.
Creates a grid of rectangles with gaps between them. Use it for planting beds, garden plots, paving, or other regular layouts.

Scale 2.0Gap Size 0.05 Scale sets the number of tiles. Lower values give fewer, larger tiles. Higher values give more, smaller ones. The default of 2 makes very small tiles on most surfaces, so lower it first if you cannot see the pattern. Gap Size sets the width of the empty strips between tiles, up to 0.125.
Width 0.5Height 0.5 Set the shape of each tile. Equal values make squares. Raise Width for long beds, or lower Height for narrow strips.
Uses an image as the mask. White areas keep instances and black areas remove them. Paint your own mask in an image editor, or use a graphic such as a logo.

Default offBounds Clip Turn on Image and choose an image file with the folder button. The layer stays empty until you pick an image. Bounds sets what happens outside the image. Set it to Clip to show the image once and leave the rest of the surface empty, or to Repeat to tile it across the surface. Use small instances and sufficient density for detailed shapes. If the outline looks rough, raise Density and lower Uniform Scale.

Min 0Max 1Sharpen offInvert off Turn on Invert to reverse the mask, so instances fill the areas that would be empty. Min and Max control the grey areas. Instances are removed below Min, full size above Max, and scaled in between. Turn on Sharpen to make soft edges crisper. These three settings do little on a pure black-and-white image, since it has no grey. Use them with gradients, photos, or softly painted masks.

Scale 1 / 1 / 1 Location moves the image across the surface, in metres. Rotation turns it; use Z to rotate it across the ground. Scale works in reverse: a larger value makes the image smaller, and a smaller value makes it larger. At 1, the image is about 10 m wide. The image keeps its proportions unless you give X and Y different values to stretch it.
Noise, Lines, and Tiles each have transform controls to move and turn their pattern.

Location moves the pattern across the surface. It moves the mask, not the instances themselves. Scale stretches the pattern along each axis. For example, stretching noise along X turns round patches into long bands. Rotation turns the pattern. Use Z to rotate it across the ground.
Use Rotation to set the direction of the rows. Location slides them, much like Phase Offset.
Use Location to line the grid up with the edges of the surface, and Rotation to change its angle.
Select a group to open Group Texture Masks. The pattern applies to every layer in the group, so they all share the same patches, rows, or grid.
Dynamics adds movement over time. Play Blender's timeline to preview it.
Makes a layer's instances sway. Wind is off on new layers.

Default No Wind Wind-Performance is the fastest. It tilts and rocks each instance as a whole. Wind-Semi-Realistic adds waves of wind moving across the layer. It balances detail and speed. Wind-Realistic bends plants along their height and adds fine flutter. It gives the most detailed motion but is the slowest, so save it for layers seen up close. Adjust Strength to the scale of your assets. Wind moves instances by a set distance in the scene, so a value that suits a large tree can bend small plants too far. Lower Strength if plants bend too much or lie flat.

Direction 0°Strength 2Speed 1Scale 2 Direction sets the compass direction the wind blows toward. Strength sets how far instances are pushed, and Speed how fast they sway. Scale sets the size of the gusts. Lower values make large areas move together. Higher values make neighbouring instances move more differently. Wind-Performance also has Smoothness, which softens the motion.

Bending 1Minor Wind on, 1 Bending sets how much a plant curves along its height instead of tilting stiffly. The Enable Minor Wind checkbox adds finer motion on top of the main sway. Minor Wind Strength sets how strong it is. In the Advanced panel, Height Falloff and Width Falloff control the effect from base to tip and from centre to edge. A Vertex Group can limit the effect to part of the mesh.

Presets Gentle Breeze, Windy, Storm Pick a preset from the Preset list and click the Apply Preset button to set Strength, Speed, and Scale for the current Wind Type. Use it as a starting point, then fine-tune it for your assets. Gentle Breeze is a light sway, Windy is stronger, steady movement, and Storm gives heavy leaning and gusts. Presets differ between Wind Types, so apply the preset again after changing the type.

Wind is calculated on every frame, which can slow playback on dense layers. The Bake Wind button stores the animation, so Blender only has to play it back. In one test with thousands of trees, playback went from about 3 to 30 frames per second after baking. Your results depend on the scene. Click the Animation button to bake the whole frame range, or Still for the current frame only. The bin icon deletes the bake. Save first and bake after final adjustments. The bake is saved next to your .blend file. If you change the wind settings, density, or frame range, delete the bake and bake again.
Animate a layer appearing or disappearing over a range of frames. There are twenty presets, and they all share the same Animation settings.

Default No Effect Pick an effect from the Preset list and play the timeline. For example: Popup: instances appear in a wave across the layer. Radial: the layer grows out from its centre. Vortex: instances spin down into place. Rain: instances fall into place from above. The other presets, such as Ripple, Geyser, and Bloom, work the same way.

Start Frame 1End Frame 60 to 90Reverse offSeed 0 Start Frame and End Frame set when the transition starts and when the layer is fully visible. A shorter range makes the effect faster, and a later Start Frame delays it. Turn on Reverse to play the transition backward, so the full layer animates out. Seed changes the order in which instances appear. Each preset also has an Effect Settings panel with its own controls, such as Edge Width for Radial.
Flattens instances near an object, such as grass under a ball, foot, or wheel.

Default offMin 0Max 0.2 Turn on Collision and pick an object in the Collision Object field. Instances near it bend down, then spring back when it moves away. Max sets how far the effect reaches from the object. The default only reaches the area right around it, so raise it to flatten a wider area. Min is the distance within which instances are completely flat. Between Min and Max, they are partly flattened.
Select a group to open Group Dynamics. Its settings apply to every layer in the group, so a whole planting moves the same way.

The Materials section, at the bottom of the Scatter tab, adjusts the materials on the layer selected in the System List. Plants from the ScatterFlow content pack are set up for these controls. For your own assets, what you can change depends on their materials.

Moves the planting through Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. The header shows the current season and how far through it you are. Season Amount sets how strong the seasonal colour change is. At 0, plants keep their original colours.

Seasons Blend 0.5Color Variation Blend 5Color Variation Seed 0 These settings stop every plant from changing colour at the same time. Seasons Blend sets how much the plants differ in seasonal progress. Lower values give a more even change. Higher values let some plants run ahead of others. Color Variation Blend sets the size of the areas that change together, and Color Variation Seed rearranges them. Leaf Randomness adds variation between individual leaves. The Season Colors colour ramp sets the colours for each season.

Default 0 Sets how much snow covers the leaves, from none at 0 to fully white at 1. Around 0.3 gives a light dusting. It is in the Seasons panel, below Season Colors. Content pack trees also have Trunk Snow Amount for snow on the bark.

Dry Mask offSpread 0.6Scale 0.15Position 0 Adds uneven patches of dry, yellow vegetation. Set Dry Mask OFF/ON to 1 to turn it on. Dryness Spread sets how much of the planting is affected, Dryness Scale sets the patch size, and Dryness Position moves the pattern. Dry/Height Amount and Dryness Height set how far up each plant the dryness reaches. Dryness Color sets its colour.

Stripe Scale 0.23Angle 0°Distortion 0 Adds light and dark bands, like a freshly mown lawn. It is on by default in lawn biomes. Stripes ON/OFF turns it on or off, and Stripe Brightness sets the contrast. Stripe Scale sets the width of the bands. Angle rotates them, and Position Offset slides them sideways. Distortion makes the edges less regular, for stripes that should not look perfectly straight. Stripe Spread Min and Max set how sharp the edge between light and dark bands is.

cards.t: Material List and the link button
cards.x: The list at the top shows the ScatterFlow materials on the selected layer. Select one to see its Main, Translucency, and Wetness settings. These control colour, light shining through leaves, and how wet the surface looks. The link button next to the Materials heading applies your changes to all listed materials. Unlink to edit a material on its own.

A biome is a ready-made set of scatter layers, with the assets, density, and masks already set up. Importing one adds its layers to your emitter as a group, which you can then adjust like any other layers.
Biome packs are installed once, from ScatterFlow's preferences. Install the content pack first, since the biomes use its models.

In ScatterFlow's preferences, choose a folder in the Biomes section, then click the Install biome packs button and choose the pack. For the full setup, see Install the biomes. Once installed, the biomes are listed in the Biome Browser, sorted into categories. To update a pack, delete its folder first, then install the new version.
Biomes saved with earlier versions of ScatterFlow still show up in the Biome Browser and import as before. New exports use the .flow format.

Choose an emitter, click the Open Biome Browser button, then click the editor you want to replace with the browser. The editor under your cursor is highlighted in blue. Press Esc or right-click to cancel. A tall area next to the viewport works best, so you can see the browser and the ScatterFlow controls side by side. The Size slider changes how large the previews are.
Click the Exit Biome Panel button, or the red cross next to Size, to return the editor to its previous view.

Type in the Search box to filter biomes by name. The Categories list sorts them by type, such as Forest or Meadow. Each installed pack has its own folder. Click a biome's star to mark it, then pick Favorites to see only your starred biomes. Favorites are kept between sessions. Use the refresh arrows after installing or exporting a biome.

Click a biome's name to add all of its layers to your emitter. They are grouped under the biome's name, so you can hide, duplicate, or adjust the whole biome at once, or change single layers. See Group Scattering. Importing the same biome again reuses the plants already in your file.

To take just one layer, click the arrow next to a biome's name to show its Individual Layers, then click the + button next to the one you want. Single layers are not grouped, which makes it easy to mix layers from different biomes.

When a biome would create more than 100,000 instances, ScatterFlow asks how to handle it in the viewport. The Yes, use adaptive safety button imports the layers hidden and lowers their viewport density. Renders are not affected. Turn the layers on when you are ready to see them. The No, keep full viewport density button imports the biome as it is. Choose this if your computer can handle it. Nothing visible after importing? Adaptive safety starts the layers hidden. Turn them on with a layer's monitor icon or the group's eye icon. If they look too sparse, raise Viewport Density in Optimization.
Save your scatter setups as biomes to reuse them in other files.

Choose Export Biome from the arrow menu below the System List. It saves every layer on the emitter, with its settings and groups, as a .flow file. In the export window, the Name and Category fields set how the biome is listed in the Biome Browser. The Partner field can be left empty. Preview Image is an optional picture for the thumbnail. Save the file inside your biome folder so the Biome Browser can find it, then refresh the browser. Use assets from your asset libraries. A biome file does not contain models; it points to them in your asset libraries. If a layer uses an object from somewhere else, the export stops and lists those objects. Replace them with library assets, or add them to a library, then export again.
ScatterFlow can import GScatter environments (.gscatter files) as biomes, without the GScatter add-on. They become ordinary ScatterFlow layers that you can edit like any other.

GScatter environments are available from the GScatter store at store.gscatter.com. Keep your downloads so you can reinstall them later. Check each environment's licence before using it commercially. Use environments, not single plants. A .gscatter file with only a plant has no layers to import as a biome.

Install .gscatter files the same way as biome packs, with the Install biome packs button. A biome folder needs to be set first; see Install the biomes. Large files can take a moment to install. You can keep working in Blender in the meantime, and Esc cancels.

Installed environments are listed under GScatter in the Biome Browser's categories. Import them like any other biome: click the name for the whole environment, or add single layers from its Individual Layers list. Each GScatter scatter system becomes one ScatterFlow layer. Large environments get the same prompt as other large biomes.

cards.t: What carries over, and what is approximated
cards.x: ScatterFlow converts GScatter's effects to the closest ScatterFlow settings, so the result looks like the original but may not match it exactly. Carried over: plants, density, seed, scale, rotation, and surface alignment. Approximated: noise masks, since several GScatter masks become one. Not imported: the GScatter terrain generator, and effects that ScatterFlow has no equivalent for. After importing, the layers no longer need GScatter.

Install biome packs is greyed out. Set a biome folder first. The file will not install. The download is probably damaged or incomplete. Download it again. The environment is not in the Biome Browser. Refresh the browser and check the GScatter category. Make sure the file is an environment, not a single plant. Some layers are missing after importing. Their plants were not found. Install the file again. If the environment uses another GScatter product, install that one too. Nothing happens when importing. Choose an emitter at the top of the ScatterFlow panel first. The scene is slow. GScatter environments can be dense. Try a smaller emitter, accept adaptive safety, or lower the density of the heaviest layers. See Optimization.
These settings make heavy layers lighter to display while you work.

Default offViewport Density 10% Shows only part of the layer's instances in the viewport. Viewport Density sets how many: at 10%, about one in ten is shown. Use it on dense layers such as grass, where a thinner preview is enough to judge placement.

Default offType Bounding Box Shows simple stand-ins instead of the full meshes in the viewport. Pick one from the Type list. Bounding Box: a box around each object. Convex Hull: a simple shell that follows the object's shape more closely. Proxy Object: a mesh of your choice, such as a cube or cone. Pick it in the Proxy Object field. Proxy Scale sets its size. Points: a cloud of points. Point Radius sets their size, and Point Density how many there are. To start new layers with Bounding Box on, turn it on in the add-on preferences.
Removes instances outside the scene camera's view. The kept area follows the camera as it moves and turns.

Default offWidth / Height 1.2Clip Start 5 mClip End 100 m Turn on Camera Culling to keep only the instances inside the camera's view and clipping range. Width and Height size the kept area relative to the camera frame. At 1, it matches the frame. The default of 1.2 adds a margin, so instances and shadows near the edges are kept. Clip Start removes instances closer than its distance, and Clip End removes those further away. Camera Culling also affects renders. Removed instances are missing from the final render too, not just the viewport. Use a generous margin, especially with a moving camera.

Default offReduction Rate 1.0Seed 0 Thins out instances the further they are from the camera. It is part of Camera Culling. Reduction Rate sets how much they are thinned, and Seed changes which ones are removed. The effect can be subtle and shows most in the distance.

Default off Removes instances hidden behind other objects, as seen from the scene camera. Turn it on and pick a collection in the Collection field. It should hold the objects that block the view, such as buildings, walls, rocks, or hills. The hidden area updates when those objects move. Camera Culling may also be required. Occlusion Culling may only work while Camera Culling is on. If it has no effect, turn on Camera Culling as well.
Lowers the polygon count of the source objects in a collection. Every instance uses those source meshes, so the whole scatter gets lighter.

In the Decimator section, pick the source collection in the Collection field and click the Add To All button. This adds a Decimate modifier to each object. Master Ratio sets how much geometry is kept across the collection. At 1, the original detail is kept; at 0.2, one fifth. The 25%, 50%, and 75% buttons are quick presets. The buttons next to Global Decimation turn the reduction on or off in the viewport and in renders, apply it permanently (checkmark), or remove it (cross). To keep editing fast without losing render detail, turn it on for the viewport and off for renders. The Collection Objects list shows each source object with its polygon count and its own Ratio, so you can keep more detail on the assets that need it.

Nano is part of the ScatterFlow build of Blender. It lowers the viewport detail of instances based on how large they are on screen, so dense scenes draw much faster. It works on ScatterFlow layers in Solid, Material Preview, and EEVEE Rendered mode, and does not affect final renders.

Turn Nano on with the button at the right end of the viewport header. In a dense desert biome with close to a million instances, the viewport redrew about 35 times faster with Nano on. Results depend on your scene and hardware.

Nano also works in Material Preview, with full materials, including displacement. In the same desert scene, the viewport went from about 0.2 to 5.5 frames per second. It also uses less memory here, because images are kept only on the graphics card once loaded.

With EEVEE as the render engine, Nano also works in Rendered viewport shading, including shadows. In the same scene, redraws went from about 6.3 seconds to under a fifth of a second. Final renders, and Cycles in Rendered viewport shading, always use the full meshes.

Click the arrow next to the Nano button to open its panel. The main button turns Nano on and off, and the other settings only work while it is on. Nano stays on or off between sessions. The Visualizer setting shows diagnostic colours. Clusters shows the triangle groups each object is drawn with, Detail shows the detail levels in use, and Instances gives each instance its own colour. Set it back to Off for normal display. In Material Preview and Rendered mode, the Visualizer only shows while Viewport Overlays are on.

Default 1 pxRange 0.25 to 8 px Sets how far the drawn mesh may differ from the full mesh, in pixels on screen. Lower values keep more detail. Higher values are faster. High values can remove fine details such as leaves, leaving the branches more visible. Use the Clusters visualizer to check the result.

Default 0 pxRange 0 to 16 px Draws fewer of the instances that are smaller than this size on screen. The smaller they are, the more are skipped. At 0, every instance is drawn. Raise it to thin out distant pebbles and small plants that add little visible detail.

Quick Tools are the two buttons at the top of the Scatter tab. They work on selected mesh objects, not scatter layers, and stay greyed out until you select a mesh. After using a tool, change its options in Blender's Adjust Last Operation panel at the lower left of the viewport, or press F9. The result updates as you change them.
Adds random variation to the size, heading, and tilt of selected objects, so repeated props look less alike.

Click the button again for a different result. Each click starts from the objects' original scale and rotation, not the last result, so repeated clicks do not keep shrinking or tilting them. Original transforms are stored for the current session. If you scale or rotate an object yourself after randomizing, that becomes its new starting point.

Scale Min 0.5Scale Max 1.0Max Tilt 15°Random Yaw on Scale Min and Scale Max set the size range. By default, objects end up between half and full size. Set Scale Max above 1 to allow larger objects. Max Tilt sets how far objects can lean from upright, up to 90°. Use 0 to keep them upright. Random Yaw turns each object randomly around its vertical axis. Turn it off to keep the original heading. Seed controls the random result. Each click picks a new seed; enter one yourself to repeat a result.
Moves objects straight up or down until their lowest point rests on the surface below. Objects above the ground move down, and objects sunk into it can move up.

The tool only changes height. It does not tilt objects to match the slope. Selected objects ignore each other, so they land on the terrain instead of stacking on top of one another. Objects with no surface below them are left where they are.

Search Distance 250 mGround Offset 0 mUse Footprint on Ground Offset leaves a gap between objects and the surface. At 0 they rest on it. Negative values sink the base slightly, which suits rocks and tree trunks. Use Footprint checks the ground under the object's centre and four corners and uses the highest point, so objects sink less on slopes. Turn it off to check only the centre. Search Distance sets how far below each object the tool looks for a surface.

The weather and atmosphere effects come with the ScatterFlow content pack. You find them in its Weather and Atmosphere catalogs in the Asset Browser. Most effects are objects you drag into the scene. Their settings are in the Modifier tab (the blue wrench) of the Properties editor. Rain Ripples and Rain Streaks are material nodes instead. Most effects are animated, so press Space to play the timeline and see them move.

Drag Drizzle, Steady Rain, or Storm from Weather > Rain into the viewport. Move and scale the effect object to cover the area you need. In the RAIN section, Rain Drop Type switches between round drops (Drop) and streaks (Line). Lines make heavy or fast rain easier to see. Rain Amount sets how heavy the rain is, and RainDrop Size sets the size of each drop. WindX and WindY, in the Wind section, push the rain sideways to change its angle. Splashes adds impacts where rain hits the ground. Turbulence varies the motion, and Optimization can limit the effect to the camera's view. Use contrast to make rain visible. Rain shows up best against a darker background. Lowering the world lighting also helps give an overcast look.

cards.t: Raindrops landing on water and wet ground
cards.x: Rain Ripples is a material node, not an object. It adds animated raindrop rings to puddles, roads, ponds, and other surfaces. Drag Rain Ripples from Weather > Rain into the object's material in the Shader Editor. Connect it to the Height of a Bump node (Shift + A > Vector > Bump), then connect the Bump node's Normal to the Principled BSDF's Normal input. Ripples are easiest to see on a material with low Roughness. Drop Amount: how many drops land. Ripple Size: the width of each ring. Ripple Strength: how deep the ripples look. Ripple Speed: how fast the rings spread. Turbulence: broader movement, like wind on the water. Group Control: the overall Speed, and Randomize for a new pattern. Ripples too subtle? Raise the Bump node's Distance. The right value depends on the size of the surface in your scene.

cards.t: Water running down glass and walls
cards.x: Rain Streaks adds animated water trails and drops to a material. Use it for windows, glass, metal panels, or wet walls. Drag SF_RainStreaks from Weather > Rain into the object's material in the Shader Editor. Then mix it with the existing material using a Mix Shader (Shift + A > Shader > Mix Shader): SF_RainStreaks Mask Output goes to the Mix Shader's Factor. Your existing material, such as a Principled BSDF, goes to the first Shader input. SF_RainStreaks BSDF goes to the second Shader input. The Mix Shader goes to Surface on the Material Output. Normal Strength, under General: how raised the water looks. Bump Strength: extra depth for the drops. Visibility: how strongly the streaks show over the material. Scale, under Mapping: the size of the pattern. Lower values give larger streaks. Location and Rotation position and orient it. A UV map is required. Streaks use the object's UVs. If it has none, add them with UV > Smart UV Project in Edit Mode. Add a sky or lights so the water has something to reflect.

Drag Snowfall, Flurries, or Blizzard from Weather > Snow into the scene. Place it above the area to cover, since the flakes fall from the effect object. Density, in the Snow section, sets how many flakes fall. Min Radius and Max Radius set the range of flake sizes. In the Wind section, Strength sets how hard the wind pushes the snow, and Direction sets which way. Simulation Speed sets how fast the snowfall runs. Accumulation builds up snow, Turbulence adds swirling, Collision lets flakes land on chosen objects, and Instance replaces the flakes with your own objects. Play from the start for accumulation. Build-up is calculated from the first frame, so jumping ahead makes the simulation catch up.

Snow Cover adds settled snow to rocks, roofs, branches, fences, and other objects. You do not need to play the timeline to see it. Put the objects in a collection, drag Snow Cover from Weather > Snow into the scene, and choose the collection in the Collission Collection field in the Snow Main section. Snow settles on the objects' upper surfaces. Where you drop Snow Cover does not matter. Snow Type switches between Volume and Island, two ways of building the cover. Try both on your objects. Snow Thickness sets how deep the snow is, and Smoothness rounds it off. Subdivision Level adds detail but is slower. Snow Pattern adds noise to the surface, and Scatter places small objects on the snow. Start with a low Subdivision Level. Detailed objects can make Snow Cover slow. Raise the level only when the final result needs the extra detail.

These presets make single objects, such as trees or flags, bend and sway. For scatter layers, use Wind in Dynamics instead. Drag Gentle Breeze, Windy, or Storm from Weather > Wind and drop it onto the object. In the Main section, Wind Strength sets how far the object bends. Direction sets the wind direction, and Wind Speed sets how quickly the gusts change. Bending sets how much the top bends compared with the base. Wind Noise Size sets the size of the gust pattern. Minor Wind adds small, fast movement for details such as leaves.

Drag Falling Leafs from Atmosphere into the scene. Pick the leaf type from the Menu list. The types range from oak and maple leaves to blossom, grass, and confetti. Count, in the Spawning section, sets how many leaves fall at once. Scale, in the Size section, sets their size, and Tumble Speed, in the Rotation section, sets how fast they spin. In the Movement section, Fall Speed sets how fast they drop, and Sway Amount and Sway Speed set the side-to-side motion. Wind Direction blows the leaves across the scene. Curve guides them along a path you draw, such as a gust down a street.

Drag Embers from Atmosphere to where the sparks should come from. Count, in the Spawning section, sets how many embers there are. Lifetime sets how long each one lasts, which also sets how high it rises before fading. The Movement section controls the rise and sway, and Wind Direction controls the drift. Embers are easier to see against a dark environment. Lower the world lighting for dusk, night, or other low-light scenes.

Dust adds tiny particles that drift slowly through the air. Use it as a subtle touch in sunlight or interiors. Drag Dust from Atmosphere into the scene. Count, in the Spawning section, sets how many particles there are. Keep it low for a subtle effect. Scale, in the Size section, sets their size. In the Movement section, Settle Speed sets how slowly the particles sink, and Sway sets the side-to-side motion. Lighting determines visibility. Dust shows up best in strong light against a dark background, such as sunlight in a dim room.

A small cloud of circling gnats, good near water or lights. Drag BugSwarm from Atmosphere into the scene. The swarm forms above where you drop it. The gnats are life-size, about 2 mm, so they are hard to see from a distance. Use a close camera, or raise Scale: 0.005 is life-size, and 0.25 makes them easy to see. Count, in the Spawning section, sets how many gnats there are. In the Flight section, Circle Radius and Circling Speed set the orbit, Attraction keeps the swarm together, and Dart Amount controls sudden darts away from the group. Match the scale to the shot. Keep the gnats small for close-ups, and enlarge them when the swarm must stay visible in a wider view.

Larger insects that flutter around one spot, such as a lamp, porch, or campfire. Drag Moths from Atmosphere to where you want them. Search for “Moth” in the Asset Browser to find it. Count, in the Spawning section, sets how many moths there are, and Scale sets their size. Wing Flutter, in the Rotation section, sets how fast the wings beat. The Flight section has the same circling, attraction, and darting controls as Bug Swarm. Both Bug Swarm and Moths can follow a path. Turn on Use Curve Path in the Curve section and choose the curve.

The Ivy tab grows climbing plants on objects such as walls, trunks, and rocks. You draw the main stems, ScatterFlow adds the vines, branches, leaves, and flowers, and you fine-tune the result in the Ivy Properties panel.

A preset gives you a plant's leaves, flowers, and growth settings in one go. The content pack includes everything from green climbers to flowering clematis. Select a preset in the Asset Browser, under Ivy > Presets in the ScatterFlow_Pro_ContentPack library. Then select your target, click Add Ivy, and draw. The new ivy uses that preset. A preset is optional. Without one, Add Ivy creates bare stems until you assign leaves. If presets are missing, see Adding the library.

Select the object to grow on. You can select several for the ivy to grow across. Place the 3D Cursor where the plant should start with Shift + Right Click, then click Add Ivy. Draw the main stems on the surface. Each stroke is one stem. Press Tab to finish and generate the ivy. Start with a few simple strokes. Your strokes are the main stems, not every vine. Branches and vines spread from them on their own, so you rarely need to draw much.
Select an ivy in the Ivy List and click Edit Ivy to change its strokes. Add stems to cover more, or delete the ones you don't want. Press Tab to regenerate the plant.

To change an ivy's preset, select a new one in the Asset Browser and click Swap Preset, the circular-arrow button between Leaf Visibility and Flower Visibility. Your stems stay; the leaves, flowers, and growth settings are replaced. To replace only the leaves or flowers, use the controls described under Changing leaves and flowers.

Type Two buttons Default Realistic Mode Realistic Mode grows stems along the surface from your strokes, with vines, branches, leaves, and flowers. Use it for plants seen up close. Fast Mode skips the stems and just covers the target with leaves and flowers. It is lighter, so it suits distant surfaces or large areas. The available settings depend on the mode. Each mode has its own settings in Ivy Properties. Ivy Bake only works in Realistic Mode.

cards.t: Leaf Visibility, Flower Visibility and the list
cards.x: The Leaf Visibility and Flower Visibility buttons show or hide those parts of the selected ivy. Hide flowers for a plant that doesn't flower, or hide both while you shape the stems. The Ivy List has one entry for each ivy in the scene. Select one to edit it. In each row, the Eye icon toggles viewport visibility, the Camera icon toggles render visibility, and the Bin icon deletes the ivy along with its stems and collections. Hover over the i icon above the list for a quick workflow reminder.

The two + buttons swap the leaf or flower meshes without changing your stems or growth settings. The left one, beside Leaf Visibility, changes the leaves; the right one, beside Flower Visibility, changes the flowers.

cards.t: Leaves and flowers from the content pack
cards.x: Select the ivy in the Ivy List. Then pick a leaf set from Ivy > Leafs in the Asset Browser and click the left +, or a flower set from Ivy > Flowers and click the right +. You can mix leaves and flowers from different plants. Use the correct replacement button. Either + accepts whatever asset is selected, so a leaf set can end up as flowers, or a flower set as leaves.

Put your leaf or flower objects in a collection. If it holds several objects, the ivy uses a mix of them. Click an empty area of the Asset Browser to clear its selection. Then select your collection in the Outliner, or an object inside it, and click the left + for leaves or the right + for flowers. The ivy keeps its overall shape. You can also set a collection directly in Ivy Properties, in the Leaf Source field of the Leafs panel or the Flower Source field of the Flowers panel. Asset Browser selection takes priority. If an asset is still selected there, the + button uses it instead of your collection. Clear the Asset Browser selection first. Place origins at the attachment point. Model each leaf or flower at the size you want, with its origin where it meets the stem. Fine-tune it with Leaf Size, Flower Size, and the rotation settings.
Expand the Ivy Properties panel to edit the selected plant. The ivy Growth panel controls its stems and branches.

Vines Spread sets how far vines reach from your stems. Raise it to cover more surface without drawing more. Branch Spread sets how far the smaller branches reach from the vines. Overall Vine Size sets the stem thickness. Vines Surface Offset sets the gap between the stems and the surface. Under Vines, Vine Density sets the number of vines, Vine Size their thickness, and Vine Seed their arrangement. Branches has the same controls for branches: Branch Density, Branch Size, and Branch Seed. Leaves and flowers grow on branches, so more branches make a fuller plant. Use seeds to try different growth patterns. Changing a seed rearranges the growth but keeps your other settings. It helps when a vine grows somewhere you don't want.

Fast Mode has no stems to edit, so its ivy Growth panel is simpler. Spread sets how far the coverage reaches across the target, in metres. Density sets how much of the surface is covered. Max Scale and Min Scale set the size range of the pieces, and Seed gives a different arrangement. The Leafs, Flowers, Wind, and Optimization panels work in both modes.

The Leafs checkbox turns leaves on or off, like Leaf Visibility. Leaf Source is the collection the leaves come from. Leaf Density sets how many leaves grow along the stems, and Leaf Spacing the minimum gap between them. Leaf Seed rearranges them. Leaf Size Min and Leaf Size Max set the size range. Leaf Rotation and Leaf Rotation2 add random rotation, and Leaf Downward Tilt Min and Max set how far the leaves tilt down.

The Flowers panel works like Leafs. The Flowers checkbox turns them on, Flower Source sets their collection, and Flower Density, Flower Spacing, Flower Seed, Flower Size Min, and Max control how they are placed. Under Flower Rotation, Flowers Rotation adds random rotation. Flowers Min and Max Upward Tilt set how far flowers turn up and away from the surface. Adjust Flower Density gradually. Presets use around 0.01, and 0.05 can already be very dense.

Turn on Wind and play the timeline to see the leaves and flowers move. Global/Wind Strength sets how far they move, and Global/Wind Speed how fast. Global/Wind Scale sets the size of the gusts. Small values make neighbouring leaves move differently; large values move broad areas together. Keep ivy wind subtle. Low strength moves the leaves without the whole plant seeming to sway away from the wall.

Viewport Density sets how many of the leaves and flowers show in the viewport, from 0 to 1. Lower it to keep a heavy scene responsive while you work. Viewport Level and Render Level set how many times the growth expands on itself. Each level adds a lot more coverage and takes more processing. Keeping them separate lets you work at level 1 and render a fuller plant. Under Advanced, Decimate Vines and Decimate Branches simplify the stems, and Vines Resolution sets how round they are. More decimation is lighter but also changes the growth pattern, so set it before you fine-tune the plant. Increase levels one step at a time. Level 3 can make a very dense plant on a large wall.
Misc has finer controls for stem variation, such as Noise Scale, Noise Strength, and Branch Offset. Sources shows the drawn curve, the target objects, and the Vines Material used for the stems.

Ivy updates whenever something it depends on changes. Baking stores the finished plant so heavy scenes play back faster. The bake controls are at the bottom of Ivy Properties, in Realistic Mode. Click the Still button to cache the current frame, for ivy that doesn't move, or the Animation button to cache the scene's whole frame range, including wind. Then click Bake Ivy. The Bin button deletes the bake so the ivy responds to edits again. Save before baking, and bake after final edits. A baked ivy ignores setting changes until you delete its bake.

The River tab turns a stroke drawn on terrain into a river. It carves the riverbed, adds animated water, and can scatter rocks or other assets along the banks. Everything stays editable, so you can change the course, width, water, or bank scatter at any time.

Select the terrain, click the Draw River button, and draw the river's course in one stroke. Press Tab to generate the river. For a quick reminder of the workflow, hover over the i icon next to the River System heading. Prepare the terrain first. Press Ctrl + A to apply its scale and rotation. The terrain also needs enough geometry to carve the riverbed. A coarse mesh gives rough banks.
Click the Edit River button to change the strokes. Add a stroke to make a tributary, or delete strokes you no longer need. Press Tab to update the river.

Water flows from the start of the stroke to its end. If it flows the wrong way, reverse the stroke instead of redrawing the river. Click the Edit River button and select the stroke (A selects all, or hover over one and press L). Right-click and choose Switch Direction, which is also in the viewport header's Segments menu. Press Tab to apply it. Raising Flow Speed for a moment makes the direction easier to see.
These settings are in the River Properties > River > Size panel.

cards.t: River Width, River Height and Terrain Falloff
cards.x: River Width sets how wide the river is. River Height sets the water level in the riverbed. Raise it to fill more of the channel. Terrain Falloff sets how far the terrain is reshaped around the river. Low values give steep banks, and high values give a wide, gentle valley. The Control Curves field, at the top of the River panel, shows the collection that holds your strokes.
These settings control the moving water surface. Play the timeline to see them in action.

Wave Strength sets how high the waves are, from a calm stream to rough water. Wave Speed sets how quickly they change. Flow Speed sets how fast the water moves downstream. Flow Strength sets how strong the streaks along the flow are. Foam Spread sets how far foam reaches from the banks and from objects in the water. Separate motion adjustments from material adjustments. Solid shading shows the surface shape clearly, so tune waves and ripples there. Then switch to Material Preview or Rendered shading to judge how the water looks.

Collision objects make the water ripple around rocks and other objects in the river. Put the objects in a collection, then choose it in the Collider field in the Extra Collision Objects panel. Two settings in the Water panel control these ripples. Collision Ripples Strength sets how high they are. Collision Ripples Falloff sets how far they spread from each object.

The river has its own scatter system for assets that follow its course, such as rocks, pebbles, or reeds. Scatter Collection sets the objects to scatter, such as rocks from the content pack. Scatter Amount sets how many are placed, and Min Distance sets the minimum space between them. Scatter Width sets how far from the river the assets spread. Low values keep them close to the water. Scatter Falloff sets how quickly they thin out toward the edge. Seed gives a different arrangement. In the Scale panel, Uniform Scale sizes all instances, and Scale Min and Scale Max add random variation. In the Rotation panel, Align To Surface follows the slope, and Rotation and Random Rotation set the orientation. Offset shifts the instances, for example to sink them slightly into the ground. Foam around scattered objects requires Realize All Instances. Keep it on if you want that foam. It is slower, so keep Scatter Amount modest while you edit a long river.
