The SF_River Material panel, below River Properties, controls how the water looks. Changes show in Material Preview and Rendered shading.

Water Color tints the water. Water Density sets how quickly the colour builds up. Low values give clear water, and high values give darker, deeper-looking water. Murkiness Color and Water Murkiness add a cloudy tint that hides the bottom. A brown tint gives muddy water. Wave Bump adds fine surface detail, set with Scale, Detail, Distance, and Strength. Depth darkens the deeper areas.

Foam forms along the banks and around objects in the water. Foam Color and Foam Amount set its colour and coverage. Foam Scale and Foam Detail set the size and complexity of its pattern. Foam Bump Strength and Foam Bump Distance give it depth. Caustics adds moving light patterns in shallow water. Adjust them with Caustic Amount, Caustic Strength, Caustic Speed, and Caustic Scale.
Scatter layers on the same terrain follow the reshaped ground. They do not avoid the water on their own.

cards.t: Scattering on a terrain with a river
cards.x: Choose the terrain in the Emitter field and create layers as usual. Because the river reshapes the terrain itself, the instances follow the riverbed and banks. Without a mask, plants also land in the channel. Use Curve Proximity to keep them out of the water. Use the appropriate scatter system. The river's Scatter System is for assets in or near the water. Use ordinary scatter layers for the rest of the terrain.

cards.t: Keep a layer out of the river with Curve Proximity
cards.x: The river's curve can mark an area for scatter layers to avoid. In the layer's Proximity settings, turn on Curve Proximity with Type set to Single Curve. Set Curve to SF_River Curve, found in the SF_RiverCurves collection, and keep Behaviour on Avoid. Raise Distance until the channel is clear. It is measured from the centre of the river, so use at least half the river width, plus a little more to keep plants off wet banks. Turn on Smooth Transition and adjust Transition to soften the edge along the water. Do this for every layer that should avoid the river. Tributaries are part of the same curve, so they are included. For a second, separate river, set Type to Multiple Curves and choose a collection that holds both curves. See Culling and Proximity for more on these settings.

River Resolution sets how detailed the river geometry is. Lower it to keep long rivers fast. Subdivide Level adds geometry to the terrain around the river, from 0 to 6. Raise it if the banks look blocky and you cannot add detail to the terrain itself. Each level makes the river much slower to process.

The Decals tab places an image on a surface as its own object. Use decals for road markings, signs, cracks, dirt, and other small details. Decals stay editable, and they never change the surface's own material.

cards.t: Choose an image, then place it
cards.x: Click the + button beside the Decal Objects list, choose an image, and click the Add New Decal button. Supported formats are PNG, JPG, TIFF, EXR, TGA, and WebP. Images with a transparent background give clean edges. You then place the decal in three clicks: its position on the surface, its size (move the mouse up or down), and its rotation (move it left or right). An arrow shows where it will go and which way it will face. The current step is shown in the lower-left corner of the viewport. Press Esc or right-click to cancel. Decals preserve the image's proportions. A wide image makes a wide decal. Decals face outward from whatever surface you place them on, including walls, floors, and rocks.

cards.t: A decal with normal and roughness maps
cards.x: To give a decal normal, roughness, or other maps, Ctrl-click all the maps for that material in the file browser. ScatterFlow connects them for you, so a rust stain can have colour, bumps, and shine. Each map is recognised by the end of its filename: _color, _albedo, _diffuse, or _basecolor: colour. _n, _nrm, or _normal: normal. _rough or _roughness: roughness. _metal or _metallic: metallic. _alpha, _opacity, or _mask: transparency. _emit or _emissive: emission. Map not recognized? Rename it using one of the supported endings above.

The list shows every decal in the scene, named after its image. Select one to edit it in Decal Properties. The Arrow icon selects the decal in the viewport so you can move it with G. The Eye icon hides or shows it in both the viewport and renders.

The magnet button below the + button turns on Surface Snap. While it is on, a decal you move with G slides over the surface under your cursor and turns to face outward. This lets you move a decal from the ground onto a wall without fixing its rotation by hand. Surface Snap also affects other objects. It turns on Blender's face snapping. Turn the magnet off when you are done, or other objects will snap too.
Select a decal and open the Decal Properties panel. The surface it sits on is shown at the top.

Opacity sets how visible the decal is. Lower it for faded or worn markings. Emission makes the decal glow, for lit signs or screens. Metallic and Roughness set how the decal reflects light. Low Roughness gives sharp reflections, like a sticker or wet paint. Alpha is the transparency taken from the image.

cards.t: Color Adjustment, Damage, Dirt and Blur
cards.x: Color Adjustment recolours the decal without editing the image. Hue shifts the colours, and 0.5 leaves them unchanged. Saturation sets how strong they are, and Value sets the brightness. Damage removes parts of the decal so it looks chipped or peeling. Damage Amount is very sensitive: values from 0.01 to 0.04 go from small chips to heavy damage. Scale sets the chip size, Detail, Roughness, and Lacunarity shape their edges, and Damage Position moves the pattern. Dirt adds grime. Dirt Amount and Dirt Color set its strength and colour, and Wetness and Bump add gloss and depth. It can be hard to see on small decals. Blur softens the image. At 1 it becomes a soft patch, useful for faint stains or shadows.

The Physics tab places objects by letting them fall and collide. Use it for things like rolling barrels, stacked tyres, or rocks settled into corners, which would be slow to place by hand. You can add physics to objects already in your scene, or place new ones with brushes that simulate them as you go.
Placement brushes use objects from a Source Collection in the current file.

The Source Collection field sets which objects the brushes can place, such as a collection of barrels, tyres, and rocks. The Arrow expands the list of objects. Use the Tick boxes to leave an object out of new placements without removing it from the collection. The All and None buttons tick or untick everything. The + button adds the selected scene objects or Asset Browser assets to the collection. Keep the source objects in the scene. The brushes place copies of them, so move the originals out of the camera's view instead of deleting them.
These controls work on the selected objects, including ones you placed yourself.

The Set Passive button makes objects solid without letting them move. Use it on the ground, walls, ramps, and anything else objects should land on. The Add Physics button makes the selected objects fall and collide. Use it on the objects you want to move, then play the timeline. Objects falling through the floor? Select the floor and apply Set Passive so it can receive collisions.

The Freeze button holds the selected objects where they are, but keeps them solid. Use it to lock part of a pile before adding more. New objects can still land on frozen ones. The Remove button takes the physics off and leaves the objects where they settled, as ordinary objects.
The placement brushes are called modes. They use the Source Collection and simulate objects live, without playing the timeline.

Click Start Scattering to show the mode dials in the viewport. Pick a mode by clicking it or pressing its number, 1–6. Drag a setting dial sideways to change it. Click an On/Off dial to toggle it. Press Esc or right-click to go back to the mode list. Press Esc again, or click Stop Scattering, to close the controls. The modes are Area, Precision, Push, Array, Grab, and Move.
Hold the left mouse button to place objects inside the brush circle. Objects keep spawning for as long as you hold it.
Hold still to build a pile, or drag to spread objects along a path. They fall and settle as they are added. Use short presses for controlled placement. A long press can add a lot of objects quickly.
Sets how many objects each brush step adds. Higher values give a denser result in the same time.
Sets the size of the area objects appear in. A small radius makes a tight pile; a large one spreads the same objects wider. Hold F and move the mouse to change it.
Set the range of random sizes. Set both to 1 to keep every object at its original size.

Sets how high above the surface objects spawn. At 0 they start on the ground. Higher values drop them from above, so they fall, bounce, and roll more before settling. Turn on Align to Surface to tilt the brush circle to match the surface under it.
When it is off, objects spawn upright. Turn it on to start each one at a random angle, so they settle on different sides.

Hold Ctrl and drag to remove objects under the brush. Click the Randomize dial to give the objects placed by the brushes a new variation. The Randomize Selected dial does the same for the selected objects only.

Click to place one object at the cursor. Press Q, or use the Next Asset dial, to switch to the next object in the Source Collection. Shift + click places another copy of the same object. Scale Min, Scale Max, Height Offset, Align to Surface, and Random Rotation work as in Area mode. Turn on Skip Rigid Body to place objects without physics, so they stay exactly where you put them, even above the ground with Height Offset. Hold Ctrl and drag to erase, and use F to resize the eraser.
Use these modes to rearrange objects already placed in the scene.
Drag with the left mouse button to sweep objects along, like a broom. Push Width sets how wide the sweep is. Hold F and move the mouse to change it.

Hold the left mouse button to pull objects toward the centre of the brush, and drag to carry them along. Use it to gather scattered objects into a pile. Grab Radius sets the area affected. Negative Strength values attract objects.

Positive Strength values push objects away from the centre of the brush. Damping slows objects down. Lower values let them travel further after a push. Adjust Strength gradually. High positive values can throw objects a long way.
Drag an object to move it. When you let go, it rejoins the simulation at its new spot.

Array repeats one object in a regular pattern, such as stacked crates or a ring of tyres. Its settings are in the sidebar under Modes, not on dials. Select the source object, choose the Array mode, and click Add Array. Set Array Type to Grid for rows and stacks, or Radial for rings. In the Count panel, Grid uses X Count, Y Count, and Z Count. Radial uses Radial Count for objects per ring, Radial Rings for the number of rings, and Z Count for layers. The Spacing panel sets the gaps along each grid axis. Radial uses Ring Spacing and Start Radius instead. In the Scale and Rotation panels, Base Scale and Base Rotation set the starting size and angle. Random Scale Min, Max, and Random Rotation add variation. In the Advanced panel, Realize Instances turns the instances into real geometry.

ScatterFlow sorts physics objects into collections, listed under Sources with a count for each: Quick Spawn: placed with the brushes. Active Rigid Bodies: given Add Physics. Passive Rigid Bodies: given Set Passive, such as the ground. Frozen Objects: held in place with Freeze. Click a collection's Arrow to select everything in it, for example before Freeze, Remove, or Randomize Selected. The Eye icon shows or hides the collection.

cards.t: From loose objects to a scatter layer
cards.x: The Convert to Scatter button turns your placed objects into instances on a new layer called Physics Scatter. They keep their positions, rotations, and sizes, and your scene is lighter than with many separate objects. Select an Emitter in the Scatter tab first, since the new layer needs one to belong to. Then click Convert to Scatter and confirm. To convert only part of the arrangement, select those objects first. The new layer is a Manual layer, so you can keep refining it with the Manual Mode brushes. Conversion ends their physics simulation. Finish settling and arranging the objects before you convert them.

These settings control how objects behave when they touch. The Collision Type menu sets the shape used for collisions. Convex Hull follows the outer shape and suits many objects. Box, Sphere, Capsule, and Cylinder are simpler and lighter. Mesh follows the surface closely; use it for hollow objects that other objects need to fall into. Friction is resistance to sliding; lower values let objects slide more. Bounce sets how much objects rebound when they hit something. Collision Margin adds an extra collision boundary around each object. Rolling and Spinning resist those motions. Raise Rolling to help barrels settle instead of rolling on. Friction Anchor helps steady stacks that slowly slide apart. The Set as Default button uses the current values for objects you add physics to later. The Apply to Selected button applies them to the selected objects. Contact behaviour depends on both surfaces. Set Bounce and Friction on the ground as well as on the falling objects.

cards.t: Split Impulse, PyBullet Solver and Origin Tools
cards.x: Split Impulse stops objects that start out overlapping from being thrown violently apart. Leave the Enable Split Impulse checkbox on. Rigid Body Cache sets the frame range when you simulate on the timeline. The settings in the PyBullet Solver section trade accuracy against speed. Raise Iterations and Substeps if small or fast objects pass through surfaces, or if stacks will not stay still. The other solver controls fine-tune difficult contacts. In the Origin Tools section, the Center of Mass (Vol) button moves each origin to the object's centre of mass, so it tumbles more naturally. The Bottom Center button puts origins at the centre of each object's base, which makes placing them on surfaces easier.

ScatterFlow connects Blender to an open Unreal Engine or Godot project, so you can send your scene straight to the engine without exporting and importing files. Objects such as rocks, buildings, and terrain arrive with their materials. Scatter layers arrive as editable ScatterFlow layers, not thousands of separate objects, so you can keep adjusting them in the engine. Exporting again updates what you sent before instead of making duplicates.

cards.t: Pick the engine and click Connect
cards.x: First open your project in the engine with the ScatterFlow plugin enabled. In Unreal, click ScatterFlow in the main toolbar. In Godot, open the ScatterFlow Pro dock. Then click the Unreal or Godot button at the top of Blender's Export tab and click Connect. The status light is green when you are connected, orange while connecting, and red when not connected. Click Disconnect before switching to another engine. Connection remains red? Check that the engine plugin is running. Then make sure the Link URL field in ScatterFlow's Export preferences matches the address shown in the engine's ScatterFlow panel.

cards.t: Tick what you want to export
cards.x: The two checkboxes under Export choose what is sent. Selected Objects sends the objects selected in the viewport. Its count shows which are new and which were sent before and will be updated. Scatter System sends the layers ticked in the Scatter Layers list. The All and None buttons tick or untick every layer. Excluding a layer does not delete it from the engine. It just skips that layer's update, so untick layers you have not changed to make the export quicker.

Click Export to Unreal or Export to Godot. Objects and scatter layers can be sent in the same export. Keep working in Blender and export again whenever you want to update the engine. Anything you sent before is updated in place, not duplicated.
Click Settings beside the Export title for optional controls. The defaults suit most scenes.

For objects The Materials checkbox sends the object's materials. Turn it off if you will build the materials in the engine yourself. The Collision checkbox adds collision, so characters can stand on surfaces and are blocked by solid objects. Nanite (Unreal only) turns on Unreal's Nanite, which suits detailed meshes. For scatter layers The Emitter checkbox sends the terrain the layers sit on. Turn it off when the terrain is already in the engine and only the layers need updating. Nanite (Unreal only) turns on Nanite for the terrain and the scattered assets. The PCG Mode menu sets how a layer starts out in the engine. Exact Mode keeps the instance positions from Blender. Procedural Mode lets the engine regenerate the scatter, so you can adjust density and distribution there. You can switch modes later in the engine.

cards.t: What is sent, and what is not
cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Export sends the content listed below. Anything else needs to be set up in the engine.

cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Selected mesh objects, with their materials and optional collision. Materials are baked when needed (see Texture Baking). Lights, except sun lamps. Collection instances arrive with the collection's meshes. ScatterFlow scatter layers, with their instances. Very large layers, over 1,000,000 instances or 500,000 for Godot, are streamed in around the camera. Ivy and water bodies made with ScatterFlow. Objects set to show only in shadows (Camera off, Shadow on, under Object Properties > Visibility) stay shadow-only in the engine. Objects turned off for rendering arrive hidden.

cards.t: Not sent: set these up in the engine
cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: The World: sky, HDRI, sky light, exposure, and view transform. Set these up in the engine, or use ScatterFlow Sky in Unreal. Sun lamps and fog boxes: use the engine's own sun and fog. Weather: turn on rain and snow with the engine's ScatterFlow controls. Rivers: water bodies are sent, but river systems are not.

cards.s: What is sent, and what is not
cards.x: Only ScatterFlow layers are sent as scatter. Particle systems, other Geometry Nodes setups, and instances from other scatter tools are left out. Convert them to real objects or bring them into ScatterFlow first. GScatter environments can be imported as Biomes. OpenVDB volumes are also left out, and the export log lists them.

Some Blender materials, such as those with procedural textures, colour ramps, or mixed shaders, cannot be rebuilt in the engine as they are. ScatterFlow turns them into image textures during export. This is called baking. The settings are in the Texture Baking section, below the Export button. Its header shows which mode is active: Auto, Bake All, or Off. The Bake on Export if not PBR toggle bakes only the materials that need it. It is on by default and suits most scenes. The Bake All toggle bakes every material, including image-based ones. Use it when a material looks different in the engine than in Blender. The Resolution buttons set the size of baked textures. Source matches the material's own images. 2K and 4K are sharper but make larger files. Raise Samples if baked textures look grainy. Timeout per Pass (min) limits how long one bake pass may take. If a pass runs over, the object is exported without baking. See When a bake is skipped or fails. Initial exports can take longer. Baking happens during export. Later exports reuse the baked images unless something has changed.
This section explains what gets baked, where the results are kept, and what a baked texture cannot hold.

Materials made of image textures plugged into a Principled BSDF are sent without baking. The engine rebuilds them from those textures. Other materials are baked. This includes procedural textures, Color Ramps, Mix Shaders, shaders other than Principled BSDF, and node groups that change their inputs. Two kinds of extra nodes do not cause a bake: Simple image adjustments, such as tiling, offset, tint, brightness, contrast, or roughness changes. The engine applies these itself. Inactive operations, such as a Mix at factor 0, a Bump at strength 0, muted nodes, or groups with no influence. ScatterFlow looks past them to the textures underneath.

Each material channel, such as Base Color, Roughness, and Normal, is baked into its own image. Bump and normal maps are combined into the baked normal map. Baking runs in the background, so you can keep working in Blender, and a failed bake will not close your session. A progress card in the viewport shows how far it has got. Press Esc to cancel. Baking uses the GPU set in Blender's Preferences > System, or the CPU if no GPU is set. You can also choose the device with the Device buttons under Texture Baking in ScatterFlow's Export preferences.

Baked images are saved in a _BakeCache folder in the export's Sync Folder, which is next to your .blend file by default. Later exports reuse them unless the material, the UVs, or the bake settings change. Objects that share a UV-based material, such as tree variants with the same leaves, also share one bake. To force a full rebake, delete _BakeCache before exporting.

cards.t: Ground materials that blend two textures
cards.x: Terrain materials often blend two tiling textures, such as grass and dirt, with a mask. Baking all of that into one image would lose detail across a large terrain. Instead, ScatterFlow bakes each texture as a tile and sends the mask separately, and the engine blends them. For this to work, each texture set must use one Mapping node with no rotation, the first UV map, and nothing based on position or normals.

Baking uses the object's first UV map, the same one the engine uses. UVs outside the 0–1 range are wrapped, so repeating textures such as tiled bark or planks bake correctly. UDIM materials are baked into one image, so their tiles overlap. The export log warns you when this happens.
Node groups are fine, but some material effects cannot be stored in a baked image.

cards.t: Node groups, nested groups and layered shaders
cards.x: Baking works through node groups and nested groups, so there is no need to ungroup a material before exporting. Layered materials, such as rock, moss, and dirt blended with masks, are baked as their combined result. Material Outputs inside groups are found too.

cards.t: Nodes that depend on the camera or the lighting
cards.x: Fresnel, Layer Weight, Light Path, Camera Data, and Ambient Occlusion can change with the view or lighting. A bake freezes them, so they no longer react to the camera in the engine. The exception is glass transparency driven by Fresnel or Layer Weight. ScatterFlow rebuilds this in the engine instead of baking it.

cards.t: Variation per copy or over time
cards.x: Per-object variation: Object Info (such as Random or Location) and Particle Info can give each copy its own colour in Blender. Copies share one baked image, so this variation is lost. Use separate mesh variants, or the engine's per-instance variation controls. Animation: animated material values are baked at the current frame, so the animation is lost.

Displacement: material displacement does not change the shape of the exported mesh. Procedural displacement is baked into the normal map as surface detail instead. An image height map on its own does not cause a bake. Volume shaders: not baked. Set up fog and other volume effects in the engine. Rain ripples and wetness: ScatterFlow's weather effects are left out of the bake. The engine's weather system adds them live.

cards.t: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: A failed bake does not stop the export. The material is sent with whatever textures and values it has. After exporting, the status bar sums up the result. The Info editor lists any skipped objects and why. For full bake details, open Window > Toggle System Console.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: The object has no UV map to bake onto, so its procedural materials are sent without baking. Fix: unwrap the object in Edit Mode, for example by choosing UV > Smart UV Project from the menu, then export again.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: The first UV map has broken values, often from an import or a modifier. Fix: unwrap the object again with UV > Smart UV Project or Unwrap. If a modifier creates the UVs, apply it and check the result in the UV Editor.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: A bake pass took longer than Timeout per Pass, so the object was sent without baking. Fix: raise Timeout per Pass. Dense meshes, 4K output, high Samples, and CPU baking all make bakes take longer.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: GPU not configured: check Edit > Preferences > System > Cycles Render Devices, and bake on a GPU rather than the CPU where you can. Bake settings: Samples 4 is enough for most materials. Source resolution keeps your textures at their existing size. A 4K bake takes about four times as long as 2K. First export: nothing has been baked yet. Later exports only bake what has changed.

cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: The material is missing an image, often after moving a scene to another computer. ScatterFlow looks for it next to the .blend file and in a textures folder there. Fix: choose File > External Data > Find Missing Files from the menu, pick the folder with the textures, and export again.

cards.t: Grainy, blurry or different from Blender
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: Grainy: raise Samples. Blurry: raise Resolution. Source uses the largest image in the material, or 1K for fully procedural materials. Different appearance: turn on Bake All, so the material is baked instead of rebuilt from its textures. If it still looks different, see the limits under Complicated materials and node groups.

cards.t: An object is not baked at all
cards.s: When a bake is skipped or fails
cards.x: Only mesh objects are baked. Curves, text, and other object types are sent without baking. Fix: convert the object by choosing Object > Convert > Mesh from the menu. Work on a copy if you want to keep the editable original.

Player Preview lets you walk through your Blender scene from a player's view before exporting. It does not need the engine or a connection. Place the viewport where you want to start, then click the Preview button in the Player Preview section. A shortcut card lists the controls: W A S D moves, the mouse looks around, Shift runs, Space jumps, and Ctrl crouches. V switches between first-person, third-person, and top-down views. The mouse wheel sets the camera distance in third-person and top-down views. Hold the right mouse button to zoom. H hides the shortcut card. Esc ends the preview and returns to your previous view. The Settings section below Preview sets the starting camera and position (such as the current view or the 3D Cursor), full screen, movement speed, mouse sensitivity, and collision with scattered objects.

Movement speed stays the same whatever your frame rate, down to 20 frames per second. Below that, the character slows down: at 10 frames per second it moves at half speed. Make the viewport faster rather than raising Walk Speed. What makes a scene slow to draw Scatter density: lower Viewport Density or use Nano; see Optimization. Renders keep their full density. Complex meshes: detailed assets repeated many times. Use lighter meshes or proxies while editing. Modifiers: Subdivision Surface, Geometry Nodes, and other modifiers that recalculate. Animation: armatures, drivers, simulations, animated objects, and wind. Shading: heavy materials, lights, or textures in Material Preview or Rendered shading. Other applications: an open game engine or another 3D app shares the GPU. Preview settings: turn on Fullscreen Preview, and leave Collide with Scattered Objects off in dense scenes.

The ScatterFlow plugin adds a panel to the Unreal Editor. Use it to bring your Blender scene over, edit scatter layers, and add environment tools. Connect Blender and Unreal. Send content from Blender's ScatterFlow Export tab straight into the open level. There is no need to import files by hand. Edit scatter layers in Unreal. Each Blender scatter layer arrives as one ScatterFlow actor that holds its instances. Select it to change density, scale, meshes, or placement without going back to Blender. Add environment tools. Add foliage wind, a dynamic sky, weather, water, and ivy. Use Play to walk around the level with a ready-made character.
The plugin needs Unreal Engine 5.8 on Windows and ScatterFlow for Blender. Install it into each project's Plugins folder separately.

Close the project in Unreal first, then: 1. Extract ScatterFlow_UnrealPlugin_V1.0.zip to a short path, such as C:\Temp. Long paths can cause problems on Windows. 2. In the project folder that holds the .uproject file, create a Plugins folder if there is not one already. 3. Move the ScatterFlowUnrealSync folder into Plugins. The file Plugins\ScatterFlowUnrealSync\ScatterFlowUnrealSync.uplugin should exist, without an extra ScatterFlowUnrealSync folder in between. Open the project. The plugin comes precompiled, and the plugins it depends on are turned on for you. In Edit > Plugins, check that ScatterFlow Unreal Sync is enabled. If you have to enable it, click Restart Now. Once it is running, the ScatterFlow button is in the main toolbar. Continue to Step 1.

Close Unreal and delete the old Plugins\ScatterFlowUnrealSync folder, then install the new version with steps 1–3. Removing the old folder first makes sure no outdated files are left behind. Update the Blender add-on at the same time, so both sides are on the same release.

cards.t: If the plugin does not load
cards.x: Modules are missing or were built for another engine version. This build of the plugin supports Unreal Engine 5.8 only. The ScatterFlow toolbar button is missing. Check that the plugin is enabled and that its folder is not nested one level too deep. Blender cannot connect. Both programs must be open. Check that Blender's connection address matches the plugin's Link Settings. See Step 2.

Click ScatterFlow in the main toolbar, next to the Play controls, to open the panel. It is also under Tools > ScatterFlow Scatter. The panel is a floating window that can stay open while you work. The top of the panel holds the Play button, which starts a walkthrough with the ScatterFlow character (see Play). Next to it are the connection status and the Link Settings button, which opens the Blender connection settings. When no layer is selected, the panel shows the scene tools. Its four icons add water, ivy, weather, or sky. The panel follows your selection. Select a ScatterFlow layer to edit its settings. Click empty space to return to the scene tools.
The connection starts when Unreal opens. In Blender's Export tab, click the Unreal button, then click Connect. The panel's status shows when Blender is connected.

Click the Link Settings button to show the connection controls. The defaults work for most projects. The status line shows whether the link is connected, waiting for Blender, or offline. Blender connection URL is the address Blender connects to. It must match the Unreal Link URL in Blender's ScatterFlow preferences. If you change the port, click the Copy URL button to update the address in Blender. Only change Port if another program is using the same one. Stop the link first, because the field is locked while the link is running. The Start with Unreal checkbox starts the connection when the project opens. Leave it on for normal use. Turn on Auto-import scatter exports from Blender to also pick up scatter exports that were saved while the connection was off. Exports sent over a live connection always arrive. Turn on Live sync edits to Blender to send your changes to linked objects back to Blender as you make them. The Mirror deletes to Blender checkbox also deletes the linked Blender object when you delete it in Unreal. It is off by default, so you do not delete Blender content by accident. The Stop Live Link button stops the connection.

Options take effect as soon as you change them, and they are kept when you reopen the project. Turn on deletion syncing only on purpose. Live sync is useful when you refine placement in Unreal. Keep Mirror deletes to Blender off unless deleting in Unreal should also delete in Blender.

Click the Stop Live Link button to close the connection, and the Start Live Link button to open it again. Blender does not reconnect on its own. Click Connect in its Export tab again to restore the link.
Once connected, click Export to Unreal in Blender. Supported content is added to the level that is open in Unreal. See Export for what to export and how.

Unreal creates the incoming assets and places your scene in the level. In the Outliner: The scatter surface becomes a terrain mesh with its material and collision, such as SF Terrain - Meadow. Each scatter layer becomes one actor holding that layer's instances, such as SF Scatter - Trees. Objects you selected individually in Blender keep their own names. Exporting again updates the existing actors instead of adding duplicates. Layer settings can keep your Unreal edits. When you export again, settings you changed in Blender replace the Unreal values. Settings you did not change in Blender keep your Unreal adjustments. The mesh list works differently; see Scatter Layers.

cards.t: Select a layer to edit it
cards.x: Click an instance in the viewport to select its whole layer and show its controls in the panel. Ctrl+click an instance from another layer to edit both layers together. Click empty space to go back to the scene tools.

Select actors in the level, expand the Export section, then click Export to Blender. Actors that came from Blender update their original Blender objects. Meshes made in Unreal arrive as new Blender meshes with their materials, so you can bring a prop built in Unreal into your Blender scene.

Turn on Live sync edits to Blender in Link Settings to send edits to linked actors straight away, without exporting each change. For example, moving a linked object in Unreal also moves it in Blender.
Settings you change in Unreal show a round-arrow button, Reset to the value from Blender. Click it to return that setting to its imported value.

The two mode buttons choose how the layer is placed. Blender Exact keeps the instance positions from Blender. Use it when placement must match the original, especially for layers you arranged by hand. Procedural rebuilds the scatter in Unreal with its PCG system. It adds density, spacing, and mask controls, and lets the layer follow changes to the ground. The panel only shows the settings for the current mode. Switch back to Blender Exact at any time to return to the imported placement.

These change the imported instances without creating a new layout. Z Offset (cm) moves every instance up or down. Use it to fix floating bases or exposed roots. Keep Ratio (thinning) sets how many instances are kept, chosen at random. At 1 every instance stays; at 0.5 half of them do. Use it to thin a layer without changing positions.

Scale Multiplier scales all instances relative to their Blender size. At 1 they are unchanged. Random Scale Min and Random Scale Max add a random size factor between the two values. Set both to 1 for no extra variation.

Rotation X / Y / Z (deg) rotates all instances. Use X or Y to lean the layer, and Z to turn it. Random Spin (+/- deg) adds a random turn around each instance's up axis, up to the angle you set in either direction.

The Meshes section lists the layer's source meshes and how many instances use each one. To replace a mesh, click its name and pick a new asset. You can also select a mesh in the Content Browser or Content Drawer, then click the arrow beside the name. The folder button finds the current mesh in the Content Browser without replacing it. Replacing a mesh updates every instance that uses it. Re-exporting replaces the mesh list. The next export from Blender brings back Blender's list. Make lasting mesh changes in Blender.

In Procedural mode you can add meshes to the layer. Pick one from the Add Mesh asset picker to add it. The Add Selected from Content Browser button adds every static mesh selected in the Content Browser or Content Drawer. Weight sets how often a mesh is used compared with the others. A mesh with a weight of 3 is used three times as often as one with a weight of 1. Meshes added in Unreal can be removed with their x button. Meshes from Blender cannot be removed here.

Ctrl+click instances, or layer actors in the Outliner, to select several layers. Your changes then apply to all of them. This is useful for adjusting related layers together, such as trees and bushes.

The Regenerate button rebuilds the placement on the current ground. Use it after sculpting a Landscape or changing a surface's collision. The Select in Level button selects the layer actors in the level and Outliner. The Open PCG Graph button opens the graph Unreal uses to build the layer. Use it when you want to inspect or work with the PCG setup directly.
These controls are available in Procedural mode. The layer updates as soon as you change a setting.

cards.t: Surface: what the layer grows on
cards.x: The Terrain + Landscape button is the default. The layer only grows on its imported terrain and Unreal Landscapes, so objects standing on the terrain stay clear. Click Any Geometry to let the layer grow on any geometry below the scatter points. Use it when assets should also cover surfaces such as roofs or boulders.

Use this to let the layer grow on one specific object, without allowing all geometry. Select the object, Ctrl+click an instance from the layer so both are selected, then click Use Selected Actor as Surface in the Surface section. Only that object receives instances; other objects stay excluded.
Z Offset (cm) raises or lowers all instances. Use small positive values for bases that sit too low, or negative values to sink them slightly. Check the result from ground level.

Density / m² is the number of instances per square metre. It starts at the value from Blender. Density Multiplier scales the density without changing that base value. Use it to try denser or sparser versions of the layer. A top-down view makes coverage and spacing easier to judge.
Changes the random layout while keeping the other settings and the instance count. Try a few seeds to find an arrangement you like.

Min Distance (cm) sets the smallest gap between instances. Instances that are too close together are removed. Raise it to reduce clumping and spread instances more evenly. Higher values can lower the final count, even when Density stays the same.
Uniform Scale changes the size of every instance. Non-Uniform scales X, Y, and Z separately. Use Z to change height, and X or Y to change width.
Turn on Random Scale to give each instance a size between Min Scale and Max Scale, multiplied by Uniform Scale. A wider range gives more variety in size.

Turn on Align to Surface to make instances stand at right angles to the ground below them. Use it for rocks, grass, and ground cover. Leave it off for trees that should stay upright on slopes. The X and Y values in Range X / Y / Z (deg) add random tilt, up to the angle you set. Around 5–15° breaks up instances that look too evenly upright.

Turn on Random Rotation to vary which way instances face, which hides repetition. Turn it off to keep them facing the same way. The Z value in Range X / Y / Z limits that variation. At 360° instances can face any direction, and at 0 they all face the same way.
Masks limit procedural placement to parts of the surface, and are available in Procedural mode. Each mask has an Enabled checkbox, and the Invert checkbox flips the area it affects.

Use this mask to keep vegetation on flatter ground, or to keep assets on steep surfaces only. Max Slope is the steepest angle allowed, in degrees. Lower it to clear steep banks while keeping flatter ground. Falloff (deg) softens the edge of the mask. Turn on Invert to keep instances on steep ground instead of flat areas.

Use this mask for height limits, such as a tree line. Height (cm) is the highest point the layer reaches, entered in centimetres. Falloff (cm) is the height range over which the layer fades out at that limit. Turn on Invert to keep instances above the limit instead of below it.

Breaks the layer into irregular patches instead of even coverage. Scale (lower = bigger patches) sets the size of the patches. Threshold Min and Threshold Max set how much is covered and how soft the patch edges are. A wider gap between them gives softer edges. Detail adds finer variation to the patch edges. Seed rearranges the pattern without changing its other settings. Turn on Invert to swap the patches and the gaps.

Controls placement around chosen objects, such as keeping plants away from a house. Select the object, Ctrl+click an instance to add the layer to the selection, then click Add Selected under Geometry Proximity. This also turns the mask on. Distance (cm) sets how far around the object the mask reaches, and Transition (cm) softens its edge. Under Behaviour, click Repel to clear instances near the object, or Attract to keep them only near it. Click an object's x to remove it. The Clear button removes all objects added in Unreal. Objects that came from Blender stay, and are counted separately above the list.

Uses a spline to shape a path, road, riverbank, or other long region. Select the layer and click Draw New Spline. A short spline appears where the viewport is looking. Move its points to shape it, and Alt+drag an endpoint to add more points. Then select the layer again to set Distance (cm), which is how far the mask reaches on each side of the spline. With Repel, 0 clears nothing. Transition (cm) softens the outer edges. Under Behaviour, click Attract to keep instances along the spline, or Repel to clear them away from it. To use an existing actor with a Spline component, select it together with the layer and click Add Selected under Curve Proximity. When you edit the spline, the scatter updates as you release a point.

With no layer selected, expand the Wind section to set wind for the whole level. It moves ScatterFlow plants, rain, snow, water waves, and ivy. The Enabled checkbox turns wind on or off. Strength sets how far plants bend, and Speed how quickly they sway. Direction (deg) is the direction the wind blows toward. Gustiness makes the wind come in gusts instead of blowing steadily. Leaf Flutter adds small, quick leaf movement on top of the main sway. Realtime viewport required. Wind only animates in the viewport when Realtime is on. It is on by default.

Select a layer and expand its Wind section to change how that layer reacts. These values multiply the level's wind. Layer Wind Strength at 0 stops the layer moving, which suits rocks and other rigid assets. At 2 it moves twice as much. Layer Wind Speed makes the layer sway faster or slower than the level's wind.

Move the viewport to where you want to start, then click the Play button at the top of the panel. The ScatterFlow character starts on the ground below the viewport camera. You do not need to set up a game mode or a character. Use W A S D to move and the mouse to look. Hold Shift to sprint, press Space to jump and C to crouch, and press V to switch between first- and third-person views. Hold the right mouse button to zoom, and press Shift+F1 to release the mouse. An on-screen card lists these controls; press H to hide it. Click Stop in the panel to end the preview.

Pick your own character Blueprint in the Character field. Leave it at None to use the ScatterFlow character. The Start at Editor Camera checkbox starts you below the viewport camera. Turn it off to start at the level's Player Start. Turn on Apply These Settings to use the camera and movement values below. Turn it off to keep your character's own settings. The Show Controls While Playing checkbox shows or hides the controls card. Third-Person Camera: Distance, Side Offset, and Height Offset place the camera. Field of View sets the normal view, and Zoom FOV is used while you hold the right mouse button. Camera Lag and its speed set how closely the camera follows you. First-Person Eye Height sets the eye height after you switch views with V. Movement: set Walk Speed, Crouch Speed, Jump Strength, and Gravity Scale. Air Control sets how well you can steer in the air. Crouch Animation and Sprint: choose the animations, and set the stride length per loop so the feet do not slide. ScatterFlow supplies these animations, or you can use your character's own.
Set up the camera before you start Play. Raise Distance to follow further behind the character, and Height Offset for a higher view.

ScatterFlow Sky puts the sun, moon, stars, clouds, fog, and exposure in one actor. It also reacts to ScatterFlow weather, so rain and snow change the clouds and lighting. Add the sky from the panel, then adjust it in the Sky section.

Deselect any layer, then click the sun icon beside Select a layer to edit it. The first time, ScatterFlow creates the materials and textures it needs. Any sun, sky light, atmosphere, cloud, fog, or sky dome actors already in the level are turned off, so two skies do not overlap. The Remove Sky button turns them back on. Enable Realtime to preview cloud movement. You can find it in the viewport menu.
Time sets the hour. Drag it, or type a time such as 6:30 PM or 18.5. The sun, sky colour, lighting, shadows, and clouds all follow the time. The moon and stars come out after dark.

Turns the sun's path around the scene, so it rises and sets somewhere else. The time of day stays the same, and the moon and stars turn with it. Use it to choose where the light and shadows come from.
Sets the latitude of the scene. It changes how high the sun climbs, how long the day lasts, and how long twilight lasts.

cards.t: Animate While Playing and Day Length
cards.x: Animate While Playing moves the time forward during gameplay. Turn it off to keep the time fixed. Day Length (min) is how many real minutes a full day takes. A short day is handy for previewing the change from afternoon to sunset.
Click a preset button, such as Clear, Overcast, or Foggy, to set the clouds, lighting, and fog in one step. All of them are dry. For rain or snow, see Weather.
Density sets how thick the clouds are. Thin clouds let more light through, and thick clouds are darker inside. Scale sets the size of the clouds, from small formations to broad ones.
Sets the height of the cloud base, in kilometres. Low clouds look closer and fill more of the sky.
Sets how fast the clouds drift, in metres per second. They move with the level's wind. Set it to 0 to stop them.
Casts moving cloud shadows on the ground. Turn it off if you do not want the clouds to dim the sunlight below.
Sets how strong the sunlight is. Automatic exposure adjusts for brightness, so a stronger sun does not always make the whole image brighter. It often gives more contrast and deeper shadows instead.
Sets the amount of haze in the distance. Higher values hide far objects first, then nearer ones. The fog takes its colour from the sky and sun.
Lets sunlight light up the fog itself, which adds visible light and depth to the air. It stands out most with a low sun. It is off by default because it adds rendering cost.

Moon Intensity (lux) sets the strength of the moonlight. At 0, nights are very dark. Raise it to see more at night. Stars sets the brightness of the stars and Milky Way. They appear after sunset and are hidden by clouds.

The Select Sky button selects the sky actor, so you can use its full Details panel. It has more settings there, such as day and night length, day of year, moon phase, cloud colours, and exposure. The Remove Sky button deletes the ScatterFlow sky and brings back the level's previous sky.

ScatterFlow Weather adds rain or snow around the camera. It also makes the scene wet, adds puddles, or covers it in snow, without you editing any materials. If ScatterFlow Sky is in the level, it reacts to the weather. Rain brings darker light and more clouds, snow brings pale clouds and haze, and thunderstorms add lightning.

Click the rain-cloud icon beside Select a layer to edit it to start rain. The first time, ScatterFlow builds the weather assets it needs. To stop it, click the None button in the Weather section. The sky goes back to its Sky Preset.

Click a preset button, such as Light Rain, Thunderstorm, or Blizzard, to set the precipitation, surfaces, and sky in one step. Pick the closest one, then fine-tune it. The settings shown depend on the weather: rain settings for rain, snow settings for snow.

Sets how much the weather changes the sky. 1 is the normal amount, and 2 makes it stronger. At 0, it still rains or snows, but the sky stays as it is in fair weather. The fair-weather clouds come from the Fair Weather Clouds slider in the Sky section's Clouds panel. This is also the sky you see before and after the weather.

Transition (s) sets how many seconds a weather change takes during gameplay. Clouds and wetness build up gradually, and switching to None dries the scene the same way. In the editor, changes usually appear at once.

Opacity sets how visible the drops are. Drop Width and Drop Length set the size of the rain streaks. Fall Speed sets how fast the drops fall. Particle Count is the number of drops around the camera at full intensity, up to 100,000. Intensity sets how heavy the rain is. It affects both the falling drops and how wet surfaces get. The drops are easiest to judge against a dark background.
Sets how much rain and snow are blown by the level's Wind. At 0, they fall straight down whatever the wind. At 2, the wind has twice the effect.
Turn on the Splashes checkbox to add small splashes where raindrops hit the ground. Splash Amount sets how many there are. Turning Splashes off keeps the ripple rings in puddles.

Wet Surfaces makes surfaces darker and glossier and adds puddles on flat ground, without changing your materials. Turn it off to keep the ground dry while it rains. Darkening sets how much wet surfaces darken. At 0, they only get glossier. At 1, they look soaked.
Puddles sets how much flat ground is covered by water. At 0, there are no puddles. Higher values make larger pools.

Puddle waves add wind-driven movement to the water in puddles. They are easiest to see in reflections at a low angle, with falling rain and ripple rings turned off. Puddle Waves sets the wave strength. At 0, the surface is still. Wave Scale sets the wave size, from small ripples to broad swells. Wave Speed sets how fast the waves move. At 0, they stop.
Sets the strength of the rings from raindrops landing in puddles. At 0, there are no rings. To see the rings on their own, turn puddle waves off.

Flake Size sets the size of the flakes. Fall Speed sets how fast they fall. Faster snow looks heavier. Drift makes the flakes swirl as they fall. At 0, they fall straight down. Particle Count and Opacity set how many flakes there are and how visible they are.

Snow Cover adds settled snow on upward-facing surfaces. Turn it off to have falling snow that does not build up. Max Coverage sets how much is covered. Lower values leave patches, and 1 covers everything.
Sets the steepest slope that can hold snow. Lower it to clear snow from steep hillsides and keep it on flatter ground.

Patches only show when the snow does not cover everything, so lower Max Coverage first. Cover Noise Scale sets the size of the patches. Lower values give broad drifts, and higher values give small patches. Cover Edge Detail roughens the edges of the patches. At 0, they are smooth.

Dry Under Cover keeps rain, wetness, and snow out from under roofs, bridges, and dense trees. Turn it off to let the weather reach those areas too. Cover Area is how far around the camera shelter is checked, in centimetres. Shelter further away is ignored.
On by default, it shows the finished weather straight away in the editor. Turn it off to preview the gradual changes you get in gameplay, such as wet ground slowly being covered by snow.
Add lakes, ponds, oceans, or pools with moving waves, foam, and underwater effects. Start from a preset, then adjust it to suit your scene.

Point the viewport where you want the water and click the water-drop icon. A flat water body is added there. Move it to the water level you want, so it cuts into the terrain. Foam and depth colour appear where the ground meets the water, so low parts of the terrain become a lake. To add more water bodies, click the Add Water button in the Water section.
Click a preset button, such as Lake, Ocean, or Swamp, to set the colour, waves, ripples, caustics, and foam in one step. The water keeps its size and position.

Water Color is the colour of deep water. Clarity is how far you can see into the water, in centimetres, before its colour takes over. Turbidity makes the water cloudy, from clear and dark at 0 to milky at 1. Refraction sets how much the waves distort what is below the surface.

Wave Height and Wave Length set the height and spacing of the large waves, in centimetres. Wave Speed sets how fast they move. Choppiness shapes the crests, from rounded swells at 0 to sharp peaks at 1. Wave Direction sets which way the waves travel. Follow Wind makes the waves travel with the level's wind.
Ripple Strength, Ripple Size, and Ripple Speed control the small movement on the surface. Caustic Strength, Caustic Size, and Caustic Speed control the moving light patterns under the water.

Shore Foam and Shore Foam Width add foam in shallow water and around objects that cut through the surface. Crest Foam adds foam to steep wave crests. If you cannot see it, raise the wave height first.

Turn on the Underwater Look checkbox to add coloured haze, light shafts, and caustics when the camera is below the surface. Underwater Fog sets how thick the haze is. At 1, it matches the Clarity you see from above the surface. Light Shafts adds visible rays of sunlight through the water.

Turn on the Affects Character checkbox to let your character interact with the water in Play. Wading slows you down, the water carries you, deep water makes you float, and moving leaves ripples on the surface. Wade Drag sets how much wading slows you down. It reaches full strength at waist depth. Character Ripples sets the strength of the rings and foam you leave as you move through the water.
Grow climbing ivy over walls, rocks, trees, or the ground. Adjust the growth, leaves, and flowers from the panel, and use blockers to keep areas clear.

Point the viewport at a surface and click the ivy icon. The ivy grows from that spot. Ivy can only climb meshes that have collision. Move the ivy actor to change where it starts, and rotate it to change its direction.
The Add Ivy button adds another plant where the viewport is looking. The Remove Ivy button deletes the selected ivy. Press Ctrl+Z to undo it.

The Light, Overgrown, and Hanging preset buttons set the growth, leaves, and flowers in one step. The plant keeps its position, seed, and meshes. The New Seed button gives a different arrangement with the same settings.

Growth sets how much of the plant has grown, from the root outward. Vine Length sets how far each main vine reaches. Main Vines is the number of vines that start at the root. Branching is the number of side branches per metre, which sets how densely the ivy covers the surface. Climb sets the direction. 1 grows upward, 0 spreads in all directions, and negative values grow downward. Wander varies the vine paths, from straight at 0 to tangled at 1. Vine Depth sets how far the vines sit above the surface, so later growth can lie over earlier vines.

Density is the number of leaves per metre of vine. Scale sets the leaf size. Tilt sets how far the leaf tips lift off the surface. Leaf Depth layers the leaves away from the surface for a fuller look.

Use the Leaf Mesh slot to replace the built-in leaf with your own mesh. Put its stem at the origin, with the leaf pointing along +X and facing +Z. You can mix up to four meshes, and a new slot appears each time you fill one. The weight beside each slot sets how much of the mix it makes up. The arrow and folder buttons work as they do in a scatter layer's Meshes section. Check Scale after assigning your own mesh. At 1, the mesh keeps its original size, so a large mesh may need a much lower value.

Turn on Flowers to add flowers along the vines and show their settings. The Flower Mesh slot takes your own flower mesh, centred at the origin and facing +Z. It works like Leaf Mesh. Density is the number of flowers per metre where the vine flowers. Scale and Scale Variation set the flower size and how much it varies. Coverage sets how much of the vine has flowers. Tilt Random varies how far the flowers lean away from the surface. Offset sets how far the flowers sit above the surface.
Wind Strength sets how much the leaves and flowers move in the level's wind. At 0, they stay still. Wind Speed sets how fast they move, compared with the level's wind.

cards.t: Keeping ivy off windows and signs
cards.x: The Add Blocker button places a box where the viewport is looking. Resize it over a window, doorway, or anything else you want kept clear, and the nearby ivy updates to match. Select a blocker to show the Selected Blockers section, where buttons choose how it works: Grow Around makes the vines grow around the blocker. Cut Out grows the ivy as normal, then removes everything inside the box for a clean opening. No Leaves lets vines pass through, but removes leaves and flowers inside. Box or Round uses the whole box or an oval inside it. Round suits rounded windows and arches. Padding adds extra space around the blocker. The Block Selected button makes fitted blockers for other actors. Select those actors together with the ivy, then click it. The blockers follow their actors when you move them.

Expand the controls at the bottom of the Ivy section for finer control. Growth: Branch Depth sets how many times branches split again, Gravity pulls growth downward, Spacing keeps vines apart, and Hang Length limits how far ivy can hang without support. Vines: Thickness sets the thickness at the root, and Tip Thickness at the ends. Leaves: turn off Leaves for bare vines. You can also vary the leaves with Scale Variation, Young Leaf Scale (smaller leaves at the tips), Rotation Random, Droop, Tilt Random, Spread, and Colour Variation. The Add Wind To My Leaf Materials button adds ScatterFlow wind to the materials of your own leaf and flower meshes. The Use Blockers checkbox sets whether this ivy responds to Ivy Blockers.

ScatterFlow Link adds a ScatterFlow Pro dock to the Godot editor. Use it to bring scenes over from Blender, edit scatter layers, and add environment tools. Connect Blender and Godot. Send objects, materials, lights, and scatter layers from Blender straight into your open Godot scene. There are no files to import by hand. Edit scatter layers in Godot. Each Blender layer becomes a layer node under its terrain. Select one to change its density, scale, meshes, or placement without going back to Blender. Add environment tools. Add wind, water, ivy, sky, and weather. Use Play to walk through the scene with the supplied character.
The plugin needs Godot 4.7, a Godot project, and ScatterFlow for Blender. Install it into each project you want to use it in.

1. Extract the plugin .zip and copy its addons folder into your project folder, next to project.godot. If the project already has an addons folder, put scatterflow inside it with your other add-ons. 2. Open the project in Godot and let it finish importing. Then enable ScatterFlow Link in the Project > Project Settings > Plugins tab. The ScatterFlow Pro dock appears next to the Inspector. 3. Reload the project once from the Project > Reload Current Project menu. ScatterFlow raises the Global Shader Variables > Buffer Size project setting for large scatter scenes, and the change needs a reload. 4. Open a 3D scene and save it. The plugin needs a saved scene to receive content from Blender. Then continue to Step 1. Use Forward+ or Mobile for ScatterFlow water. The water does not display correctly with the Compatibility renderer. New projects use Forward+ by default. The active renderer is shown in the editor's upper-right corner.

Close Godot, delete the project's addons\scatterflow folder, and copy in the new one. When you reopen the project, ScatterFlow rebuilds its materials once if the new version needs it. Update the Blender add-on at the same time, so both sides are on the same release.

cards.t: If the plugin does not load
cards.x: ScatterFlow Link is missing from the Plugins list. The plugin must be at addons\scatterflow directly inside the project. Check for an extra folder, such as addons\addons\scatterflow or one named after the download. The dock does not appear. Make sure Enable is ticked for the plugin, then reload the project. Blender cannot connect. Both programs must be open, and Blender's connection address must match the one in Plugin Settings. See Step 2.

cards.s: Step 1: Open the ScatterFlow Pro dock
cards.x: Open the dock from the ScatterFlow Pro tab next to the Inspector. When no ScatterFlow node is selected, it shows the scene tools in these sections. Global Wind: wind for ScatterFlow plants across the project. Play: walk through the scene with the ScatterFlow character. Export: send selected nodes back to Blender. Plugin Settings: the Blender connection. The four icons at the top right add water, ivy, sky, or rain. Water and ivy are placed where the 3D view is looking. Each tool has its own page, including Wind and Play. The Sky section only appears when the scene has an SF Sky. Weather appears when there is a sky, or when rain or snow is on. The dock follows your selection. Select a ScatterFlow layer, water, or ivy node to see its controls. Click empty space or any other node to get back to the scene tools.
The connection starts by itself when you open the Godot editor. To link the two, click the Godot button in Blender's Export tab, then click Connect.

The Plugin Settings section, at the bottom of the dock, holds the connection controls and the options for linked objects. Blender Link A green Linked to Blender status means you are connected. Waiting for Blender means Godot is ready, but Blender has not connected yet. The address shown here must match the Godot Link URL field in Blender's ScatterFlow preferences, under Settings > Export > Godot. The defaults already match. If you change the address, click the Copy button and paste it into Blender. Port: change it only if another program already uses it. Then click Restart and update the Link URL in Blender to match. Objects Live Sync Edits to Blender: when this checkbox is on, it sends moves, rotations, and scale changes on linked nodes back to Blender, including linked lights and cameras. Deleting Here Deletes in Blender: when this checkbox is on, deleting a linked node in Godot also deletes its Blender object. It is off by default, so you do not lose Blender content by accident. The last status line shows the connection's latest activity.

Clicking Restart restarts the connection and drops the current link to Blender. Blender does not reconnect on its own. Click Connect in its Export tab again. Restart only when needed. Use it after changing the port, or if the connection stops responding. Otherwise the connection starts by itself with the editor.

Once connected, click Export to Godot in Blender's ScatterFlow Export tab. Godot builds the scene in two passes. First come the objects, meshes, and materials, under a node named after your Blender scene. Then each terrain becomes an SF Terrain node with collision, with its scatter layers under it. Save the Godot scene when both passes have finished. Re-export to update the scene. Existing objects are updated instead of duplicated, and scatter layers are rebuilt from the new Blender result.

Select the nodes you want to send, such as meshes, lights, cameras, or empty nodes. Then click Export to Blender in the Export section. Linked nodes update their Blender objects. New nodes create new Blender objects and stay linked for later exports and live edits.

Turn on Live Sync Edits to Blender in Plugin Settings to send edits as you make them. Moving a linked object in Godot then moves it in Blender too. Turn on Deleting Here Deletes in Blender only if deleting a node in Godot should also delete its Blender object.
Each imported scatter layer is a node under its SF Terrain. Use Blender Exact mode to keep the placement from Blender, or Procedural mode to regenerate the layer in Godot with editable settings.
Select a layer in the Scene tree to show its controls in the dock. Ctrl+click to select several layers. Your changes then apply to all of them.

The Mode panel shows the instance count. Click Blender Exact or Procedural to switch between the two modes. Blender Exact is the default. It keeps the positions from Blender and lets you thin, scale, rotate, and raise or lower them. Use it when placement needs to match Blender. Procedural regenerates the layer in Godot, with the full scatter and mask controls. It starts close to the Blender setup, but not as an exact match. Each mode keeps its own settings, so you can switch back and forth to compare.

Keep Ratio sets how many of the imported instances are kept. 1 keeps them all, 0.5 about half, and 0 hides them all. Lowering it and raising it again brings back the same instances, so the layout does not shuffle.

Scale Multiplier scales every instance from its imported size. 1 keeps the Blender result. Under Random Scale, Min and Max add random size variation on top. A wider range gives a stronger mix of sizes. Set both to 1 for no extra variation.

Offset X, Y, and Z rotate every instance by a fixed angle. Use X or Y to lean the whole layer. These controls use Z as up, like Blender. Random Yaw adds random turning around the upright axis, up to the set angle either way. Combined with a tilt, it makes tilted instances face different directions.
Z Offset moves every instance up or down, in metres. Negative values sink them into the ground. Use it to fix floating bases, lift plants that sit too low, or bury rocks slightly.
Click Procedural in the Mode panel to generate the layer in Godot. Your changes show in the 3D view right away.

Scatter On: lists the meshes the layer scatters on. When the list is empty, the layer uses its own terrain. To scatter on other meshes, such as a roof or a boulder, select them together with the layer and click Add Selected. Keeping the layer selected keeps its controls in the dock. Or click Pick… to choose a node from a list. Click Select beside a target to select it in the scene, or ✕ to remove it from the list. An empty list goes back to the layer's terrain. Target surfaces require collision. Imported terrains already have it. For your own meshes, add a StaticBody3D with a collision shape.

cards.t: Scattering: Density / m² and Density Multiplier
cards.x: Density / m²: how many instances per square metre. A value of 0.03 is about one instance per 33 square metres, while grass and flowers often use 1 or higher. Density Multiplier: scales the overall density while keeping the base value from Blender. A top-down view makes crowded or sparse areas easier to spot.
Seed gives a different random arrangement without changing any other settings. The same seed always gives the same layout.
Minimum Distance is the smallest gap allowed between instances, in metres. Instances that would be closer are left out. Raise it to reduce clumping and spread instances more evenly.
Max Instances caps the number of instances, whatever the Density. Use it to keep very large or dense layers under control.
Uniform Scale: the overall size. 1 uses the mesh's own size. Non-Uniform Scale X, Y, and Z: scale each axis on its own. Z is height, so raise Z for taller instances and X or Y for wider ones.
Turn on Random Scale to give each instance a size between Min and Max. A wider range gives more variation.

Align to Surface tilts each instance to match the ground beneath it. Turn it off to keep instances upright on slopes. Use it for rocks, grass, and ground cover. Leave it off for trees that should grow straight up.

Turn on Random Rotation to vary how instances are turned, which reduces repetition. Amount X, Y, and Z set the range for each axis, in degrees. By default only the heading around the upright axis varies. Add X or Y for random tilt.
Z Offset in the Rotation panel moves instances by a set distance, in metres. With Align to Surface off, they move straight up or down. With it on, they move along the tilted upright direction.

cards.t: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Masks limit where a layer grows, by slope, height, patterns, or distance to objects and paths. Turn a mask on with the checkbox in its title. You can combine several masks.

cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Max Angle: the steepest slope allowed, in degrees. Lower it to clear steep faces and keep instances on flatter ground. Turn on Smooth Transition to soften the edge. Transition then sets how wide the fade is, in degrees. Turn on Invert to keep instances on steep ground instead of flat ground.

cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Height: the highest point instances can grow, in metres above the terrain's origin. Lower it to clear the tops of hills. Turn on Smooth Transition to soften the height limit. Transition then sets the distance, in metres. Turn on Invert to keep instances above the limit instead of below it.

cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Breaks coverage into irregular patches, for plants that grow in clusters. Scale: the patch size. Lower values give larger patches. Detail: adds finer pattern inside the main one. Roughness: how strong that finer detail is. Lacunarity: how much the scale changes between detail levels. Distortion: warps the patches into less rounded shapes. Seed: a different pattern with the same settings. Min and Max under Range set how sharp the patch edges are. Close values give hard edges, and a wider gap gives softer ones. Turn on Invert to swap the patches and the gaps.

cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Controls placement near chosen objects. Select them together with the layer and click Add Selected under Objects, or click Pick…. Distance: how far from the objects the mask reaches, in metres. Turn on Smooth Transition and set Transition to soften the edge. In the Behaviour list, Repel clears instances near the objects, and Attract keeps them only near the objects. Use Repel to clear space around a house, or Attract for plants along its walls.

cards.s: Masking: where a layer may grow
cards.x: Uses a path to shape a region, such as a footpath or roadside planting. Add a Path3D node and draw its points in the 3D view. Then select it with the layer and click Add Selected under Curves. Distance, Smooth Transition, Transition, and Behaviour work as in Geometry Proximity, measured from the path. Infinite Height measures distance sideways only, ignoring height. Turn it on when the path sits above the terrain. Without it, raising the path can shrink or remove its effect. Paths remain editable. Moving their points updates the layer.

The Meshes panel lists the meshes the layer scatters. In Blender Exact it shows how many instances each mesh has. You can change the list in Procedural mode. Weight: how often a mesh is picked compared with the others. 0 leaves it out. Click + Selected Nodes to add meshes from the selected nodes, with their materials. Click + FileSystem to add meshes or model files selected in the FileSystem dock, such as .glb, .gltf, .fbx, .obj, or .tscn scenes. Click ✕ to remove a mesh from the layer. Re-exporting replaces the mesh list. Exporting from Blender again brings back Blender's mesh list.
Global Wind sets the wind for the whole project. Each layer then has its own controls for how it responds.

The Global Wind section is in the dock when no layer is selected. The Enabled checkbox turns wind on or off for the whole project. Strength: how far plants bend. Speed: how fast they sway. Wind settings are saved in the project and also apply in your exported game.

Select a layer and open its Wind section to set how it responds. This lets stiff bushes and soft grass move differently in the same wind. Strength: multiplies the global strength. 0 keeps the layer still, 1 uses the global value, and higher values bend it more. Speed: how fast the layer moves compared with the global speed. Gust: from a steady sway at 0 to gusty movement at 1. Direction: the direction the wind blows toward, in degrees (0° is +X). Leaf Flutter: adds small, quick leaf movement on top of the main sway.

Move the 3D view to where you want to start, then click ▶ Play from Editor Camera in the Play section. ScatterFlow saves the scene and starts the game with the character under the editor camera. You do not need to set up a player or controls. Use W A S D to move, the mouse to look, Shift to sprint, Space to jump, C to crouch, and V to switch between first and third person. Hold the right mouse button to zoom, and use the mouse wheel for camera distance. Esc releases the mouse, and H hides the on-screen controls. Press F8 or Godot's Stop button to stop.

Set up the view in the Camera section, under Play, before you start. First Person / Third Person: click one to pick the view you start in. Third Person Distance: how far behind the character the camera follows. Side Offset: moves the camera sideways for an over-the-shoulder view. Pivot Height Offset: raises or lowers the point the camera follows. Camera Switch Smoothness: how smoothly the view changes when you press V. Third Person Camera Collision: when on, keeps the camera in front of walls and obstacles instead of passing through them. Field of View and Zoom Field of View: the normal view angle, and the one used while you zoom. Mouse Sensitivity: how strongly the view responds to the mouse.

The Movement section sets how the character moves: Walk Speed, Sprint Speed, and Crouch Speed in metres per second, plus Jump Speed and Gravity. Ground Response and Air Response set how responsive movement feels. Under Body, Player Radius, Standing Height, Standing Eye, Crouch Height, Crouch Eye, and Crouch Smoothness set the character's size and how it crouches. In the Character section, Character Scale sets the model's size, and Facing Offset fixes which way it faces. Animation Speed and Turn Smoothness control its animation and turning. Play again after each change to check speed and size against your scene.

SF Sky handles the sky, sun, moon, clouds, stars, fog, and exposure in one node. The sun and moon move with the time, place, and season you set. While the sky is active, it uses its own environment and lights. Your scene's WorldEnvironment and directional lights are switched off, and come back when you remove the sky. The sky's lights are not saved as permanent scene objects.
Click the sun icon at the top of the ScatterFlow Pro dock to add an SF Sky node to the open scene. Its settings are in the dock's Sky section. A scene can have only one SF Sky.

Default 10:00 AMRange 0:00 to 24:00 Sets the time of day. You can drag the slider or type a time, such as 14:30, 2:30 pm, or 9am. The sun, shadows, and sky colours follow it. Turn on Animate to let time pass while the game runs. Day Length sets how many real minutes a full day takes. In the editor, the time stays where you set it.

Default 0°Range -180° to 180° Turns the sun's whole path around the scene. Use it to choose where the sun rises and sets, and which way shadows fall, without changing the time. The moon and stars turn with it. At 0°, the sun rises toward +X, which counts as east.

Latitude default 40°, -89° to 89°Day of Year default 172, 1 to 365 Latitude sets how far north or south of the equator the scene is. It changes how high the sun climbs and how long twilight lasts. Negative values are in the southern hemisphere. Day of Year sets the season. Day 172 is midsummer in the northern hemisphere, and day 355 is midwinter.

Default 12 daysRange 0 to 29.5 days Sets the number of days since the new moon. About 7 days gives a half moon, and 15 a full moon. Moon Age also changes where the moon is in the sky and when it rises.

cards.t: Clear, Partly Cloudy, Cloudy, Overcast, Foggy
cards.x: Each preset button sets the clouds and fog together. Partly Cloudy is the default. Clear has no clouds or fog. Partly Cloudy, Cloudy, and Overcast each add more cloud, up to a solid grey layer. Foggy has thick fog and no clouds. Choosing a sky preset also stops any rain or snow. Fine-tune the result with the settings below.

The clouds are 3D and lit by the sun. Start with a preset such as Cloudy, then adjust them here. Density sets how thick and opaque the clouds are. Scale sets their overall size. Base Altitude sets the height of the cloud bases. Lower clouds sit closer to the scene. Thickness sets how tall the cloud layer is above its base. Speed and Direction set how the clouds drift. Change sets how quickly their shapes evolve. At 0, they keep their shape as they move. Quality (steps) sets the rendering detail. Lower values are faster but can look grainy. Higher values are smoother but cost more.

These settings control how bright, what colour, and how large the sun, moon, and stars are. Sun Intensity sets the strength of the sunlight, and Sun Color tints it. Sun Size sets how large the sun looks. The real sun is about 0.5° across. Haze adds atmospheric haze. Raise it for a paler sky and softer distances. Sky Brightness sets how bright the sky is and how much it lights the scene. The Shadows checkbox turns on shadows from the sun and moon. Moon Intensity, Moon Color, and Moon Size set the strength, tint, and size of the moonlight. Stars sets how bright the stars are. At 0, they are hidden.

Fog Density sets the fog in clear weather. Small values blend distant objects into the sky. Weather Fog is the extra fog used by the Foggy preset and in rain or snow. Auto Exposure is on by default and adjusts the brightness for day, night, and storms. Turn it off to use a fixed exposure set by Exposure. Exposure adjusts brightness in stops, on top of Auto Exposure when it is on. -1 halves the brightness and +1 doubles it.

Weather can change the clouds, brightness, and fog, and thunderstorms add lightning. Click the None button in the Weather section to go back to your sky preset. Follow Weather is on by default. Turn it off to keep your sky as it is while rain or snow still falls. Influence sets how strongly the sky reacts to rain or snow. Transition sets how long the sky takes to change when the weather changes in the game. In the editor, changes are immediate. Lightning / min sets how often lightning flashes in a full thunderstorm.

The Select Sky button selects the SF Sky node, so you can edit its settings in the Inspector. The Remove Sky button deletes the sky and brings back the scene's previous environment and lights. Deleting the SF Sky node yourself does the same.
